title: Sherlock Holmes

subtitle.text: I went to 221B Baker Street to call on my friend, Mr. Sherlock Holmes.
Mr. Holmes rents a three-room flat from Mrs. Hudson.
The study, as Holmes liked to call the large sitting room, was always a bit disorderly.
When I arrived, I saw that he was talking with a stout, red-faced gentleman with fiery red hair.
"So sorry to bother you," I said.
"No bother," said Holmes.
"I don't think you could have come at a better time.
Mr. Wilson, here, was explaining the circumstances surrounding a most unusual part-time job.
Mr. Wilson, this is Dr. Watson. He has been my helper and partner in many of my most successful cases."
Mr. Wilson and I greeted each other, and I took a seat near Holmes.
Holmes was sitting with his fingertips together, which is his habit when considering a matter of importance.
"My dear Watson," began Holmes, "I know you share my love of bizarre events, and that you like to retell the stories of my adventures in exciting ways.
I think you will find Mr. Wilson's story quite stimulating."
I was indeed intrigued, and I answered, "Your cases are always interesting to me, my dear Holmes."

"Mr. Wilson was telling me his story," continued Holmes, "and, if he would be so kind, I would like him to begin again—first, to introduce you to the case, and second, so that I may better understand the details.
What I have heard so far suggests that this case may be my most extraordinary one yet."
The stout man puffed with obvious pride at Holmes' words and he pulled from his pocket a dirty, wrinkled newspaper clipping.
As he did this, I took the opportunity to examine the man, in the way I imagined Holmes had already examined him.
I didn't gain much from my survey.
To my eye, Mr. Wilson seemed quite commonplace.
He was overweight, and from his attire, I could tell he was a tradesman.
His clothing was slightly worn, and an ornamental gold chain suggested he carried a watch.
Other than his fiery red hair, I observed nothing remarkable.
Holmes, however, stated, "I can deduce nothing beyond the obvious facts that he has at some time done manual labor, has been to China, and has done a considerable amount of writing lately."
Mr. Wilson gaped at Holmes in amazement and said, "How in the world did you know all that?
It's true when I was younger, I did manual labor. I was a ship's carpenter."
"I knew from your hands. Your right hand is slightly larger than your left," explained Holmes.
"And China?" asked Mr. Wilson.
"Well, the tattoo on your right wrist could only have been done in China, and you also have a Chinese coin hanging from your watch chain," answered Holmes.
"What about the writing?" asked Mr. Wilson.
"The right cuff of your coat is worn smooth, but the left cuff is not.
There is a patch over the elbow of your left sleeve, but no patch on your right sleeve.
The combination of these facts leads me to believe that you have done a lot of writing lately," explained Holmes.
"Quite so!" exclaimed Mr. Wilson, impressed.
"I believe you were about to show us a newspaper advertisement," said Holmes.
"Yes, yes," said Mr. Wilson. "Here it is." Below is what Holmes and I read:
TO ALL RED-HEADED MEN:
The late Mr. Hopkins has left his fortune to help all red-headed men.
A vacancy has opened in the League. Members can earn a salary of four pounds a week.
All red-headed men 21 years old or older are eligible.
Apply in person on Monday at eleven o'clock to Duncan Ross at the League's office, 7 Pope's Court.
I read it again and exclaimed, "What on earth does this mean?"
Holmes chuckled and said, "Yes, my dear Watson, it's a little off the beaten track, isn't it?"
Holmes then turned to Mr. Wilson and said, "Please, tell us about your household, your occupation, and the effect this advertisement has had on your life."
"Well, this whole affair began about two months ago," began Mr. Wilson.
"As I told you, I own a small pawnshop in Coburg Square.
It provides me enough to live on, but nothing more.
I have recently hired a new assistant who agreed to work for half wages so that he could learn the business."
"What is the name of this kind youth?" asked Holmes.
"His name is Vincent Spaulding, although he's not much of a youth," answered Mr. Wilson.
"But I couldn't ask for a smarter assistant. He could easily earn twice what I pay him, but since he is satisfied, there is no sense in putting ideas into his head."
"Yes," said Holmes in agreement.
"You seem most fortunate. It's hard to get good employees these days, and you have found one for half price.
I think your assistant is almost as interesting as your position at the Red-Headed League."
"Oh, he has his faults," professed Mr. Wilson.
"Really?" said Holmes curiously.
"Oh yes. He is crazy about photography. He is always taking pictures and then running down to the cellar to develop them, but besides that he is an excellent worker."
"Is he still with you?" asked Holmes.
"Yes, he is, and I also have a young girl who does the cooking and cleaning for me. There's just the three of us."
"Do you often read the advertisements in the newspaper, Mr. Wilson?" asked Holmes.
"No, sir," said Mr. Wilson. "I usually have no need."
"Then may I ask how you learned about this one?"
"My assistant brought it to my attention eight weeks ago.
He came running out of his office saying, 'I wish I were a red-headed man. There's a vacancy in the League!'"
"So Mr. Spaulding informed you of the opening?" asked Holmes.

"Yes, exactly," said Mr. Wilson, "and I looked at Mr. Spaulding and said, 'What's this nonsense?' and he replied, 'If I had red hair like you, Mr. Wilson, I could have a part-time job that earns me four pounds a week.' 'Ridiculous,' I said.
'Haven't you heard of the Red-Headed League?' he asked.
'You, yourself, are eligible,' he said.
Now, Mr. Holmes, my business isn't doing well, so I was interested in earning a little extra money, but the idea of getting a job because my hair is red seemed absurd."
"You were skeptical about the advertisement, then?" asked Holmes.
"Oh yes," replied Mr. Wilson.
"But Mr. Spaulding convinced me. He seemed quite certain that I would get the job.
He even went with me to the League's office the next day."
It was close to mid-morning, and Sherlock Holmes and I were in the middle of interviewing Mr. Wilson about his fantastic part-time job.
He had gotten this job not because of any skill or talent, but simply because he had red hair.
He had worked there for eight weeks, and received a handsome salary of four pounds per week.
But Mr. Wilson had gone to work that morning only to find his office closed and his job gone.
He had come to Mr. Holmes looking for answers, and my friend, upon hearing the story, perceived that there was more to this part-time job than anyone had initially thought.
Mr. Wilson had just finished explaining how his assistant had brought the notice to his attention; Mr. Spaulding had even offered to accompany him to the interview.
"I see. First, your assistant convinced you that the advertisement was valid, and then, he proposed going with you to the interview," said Holmes.
"Now, can you describe the interview for me?"
"Oh, Mr. Holmes, I never want to see such a spectacle again.
Men with red hair came from every direction.
I think every red-haired man in the city of London answered the advertisement.
If I had been alone, I certainly would have returned home, but Mr. Spaulding was quite sure I would succeed."
"Indeed," said Holmes encouragingly. "Please continue."
"Well, we waited and eventually we made it inside. The office was quite bare: a couple of wooden chairs and a card table.
In the office was a man with hair redder than mine. ‘This is Mr. Wilson,' said my assistant. And the man seemed very pleased to see me.
He introduced himself as Mr. Duncan Ross and explained that the late Mr. Hopkins had been his benefactor. Then he grabbed my hair and pulled it."
"And what happened next?" I said impatiently.
"Oh, I cried out," stated Mr. Wilson.
"Mr. Ross apologized, saying, ‘Sorry, but we have twice been tricked by wigs and once by paint.'
He then shouted to those still waiting, ‘The position has been filled,' and the crowd let out a great groan.
Mr. Ross stated that he would be my manager and proceeded to tell me about the job.
I would have to be in the office from ten to two every Monday through Saturday.
Furthermore he said that I could not leave the office for any reason during that time, or I would lose the job, and while I was in the office, I should copy [i@the Encyclopedia Britannica@i]."
Mr. Wilson paused, then continued his story.
"When I told him I already had a job, he didn't seem concerned.
He simply asked, ‘Is there no one who could run it for you? A son, perhaps?
Before I could answer, my assistant exclaimed, ‘I could look after the business for you, Mr. Wilson.'
Mr. Ross said, ‘Excellent! Then it's settled.
I expect you here on Monday by ten,' and he left.
Now, a pawnshop's business is mostly conducted in the evenings, Mr. Holmes . . . especially on Thursdays and Fridays when people find themselves in need of cash.
So a part-time job in the mornings and early afternoons suited me well.
Besides I knew my assistant was a competent man, and so for the last eight weeks, I have been working my way through the encyclopedia, starting at the first volume, A.
But today it has all come to an end."
Mr. Wilson reached into his pocket and pulled out a small printed card that said:
THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE IS DISSOLVED
October 9, 1890
Holmes and I looked at the curt announcement and the bewildered face of the disappointed man who held it.
I then looked at Holmes, and Holmes looked at me.
As we stared at each other, the comical nature of the entire affair made us burst into a roar of laughter.
"I don't find this at all amusing," said our client.
"If you are only going to laugh at me, I shall go elsewhere!"
"No, no," said Holmes, gently guiding Mr. Wilson away from the door.
"I don't want to lose this case, so please excuse us.
Can you tell us what you did after reading the announcement?"
"First I asked around at some of the adjacent offices, but they were ignorant of Mr. Ross and the Red-Headed League," answered Mr. Wilson.
"I then went to the landlord, and he too had never heard of them, so I asked about the gentleman from room number four.
The landlord told me that the red-headed man's name was William Morris and that his lease had expired, so he moved out yesterday.
I asked where I could find him, and the landlord gave me the following address: 17 King Edward Street.
I was determined to find out what was going on, so I made for that address at once.
But when I got there, I found that it was an umbrella factory, and no one had heard of either Mr. William Morris or Mr. Duncan Ross."
"What did you do next? Did you come straight here?" asked Holmes.
"No, I stopped at home," answered Mr. Wilson.
"My assistant suggested that I wait for the mail.
He thought a formal letter must have been sent in the mail, but I am not a patient man, so I decided to come to you."
"Yes, that is wise," said Holmes, "for I believe something quite serious may be about to happen.
Can you tell me more about Mr. Spaulding? For example, how did you hire him?"
"He answered my advertisement," said Mr. Wilson.
"Were there other applicants?"
"Many others, but he indicated that he would be willing to work for half wages," replied Mr. Wilson.
"What does he look like?" asked Holmes.
"He is small and dynamic. And there is a small scar on his forehead."
Holmes sat up excitedly. "Are his ears pierced?"
"Yes. Do you know Mr. Spaulding?" asked Mr. Wilson, surprised.
"No," said Holmes, "but a man of that description is known to me.
I think we're finished, Mr. Wilson. I hope to have your answer by Monday."
Holmes accompanied Mr. Wilson to the door, and we said our good-byes.
"Well, Watson," said Holmes, turning to me, "can you make sense of it?"
"I can make nothing of it," I answered frankly.
"What do you plan to do?"
"Smoke," said Holmes, pulling his pipe from his pocket.
He sat down in his chair, and contemplated the problem at hand.
From experience, I knew not to interrupt him during these periods of concentration, so I read a magazine and waited.
The magazine was dull and I was feeling a little drowsy, so I was quite startled when Holmes suddenly sprang from his chair.
After Mr. Wilson left Holmes' study at 221B Baker Street, my friend sat in his favorite chair by the fireplace, smoked his pipe, and pondered the mystery of the Red-Headed League.
Suddenly Holmes burst from the chair like a jack-in-the-box, placed his pipe down upon the table, and, turning to me, said, "There is a concert this afternoon at St. James' Hall.
Could your patients spare you for a few hours?"
"I have no more appointments today," I answered.
"Then put on your hat and come.
We'll go through the city and have lunch on the way.
The program looks excellent."
I have known Holmes for years, so I knew not to question his plan.
What may seem strange or trivial to me always turns out to be appropriate and a significant part of the case.
We traveled by the Underground. When we got off, we walked a short distance to Coburg Square.
It was a shabby neighborhood. On one of the buildings there was a sign: Wilson's Pawnshop.
Holmes and I approached the building.
First, Holmes studied it carefully; then, he walked up and down the block and studied each of the other buildings in the neighborhood.
When he was satisfied, he returned to Mr. Wilson's building.
He struck the pavement two or three times with his walking stick, and then he went up to the door and knocked.
The door was opened by a bright, clean-shaven fellow, who said, "Step in, please."
"Thank you," said Holmes, "but I'm in need of directions. How can I get to the Strand Theater?"
"Take that street over there, then take the third right, and then the fourth left," answered the assistant and promptly closed the door.
"Smart fellow," said Holmes as we walked away.
"In my opinion he is the second smartest man in London, and if I end up being wrong about him, he will have every right to be called the first."
"You know him?" I asked.
"I know of him, but this is the first time our paths have crossed," answered Holmes.
"Mr. Wilson's assistant certainly plays a major role in this mystery, so you asked for directions to the Strand in order to look at him," I said.
"Not him," said Holmes.
"What then?" I said, surprised.
"The knees of his pants," answered Holmes.
"What did you see?" I inquired.
"What I expected," said Holmes mysteriously.
"Why did you beat the pavement?" I asked.
"My dear doctor," replied Holmes almost inaudibly, "this is a time of observation and reflection, not talk."
When we got to the Strand Theater, Holmes stopped and said, "Sorry to have been so abrupt, but we were spies in the enemy's territory.
It was risky to talk about the case back there.
Now that we know something of Coburg Square, let us explore more of this neighborhood."
The Strand Theater is on one of the main roads of the city, a diagonal road that allows traffic to flow north west across the city.
We followed this main street back in the direction of Coburg Square.
"Let me see, we've passed through three intersections," said Holmes.
"Yes, this is about right."
It was difficult to believe that this busy street is so close to the faded, stagnant, and forgotten Coburg Square.
"I'd like to remember these buildings exactly," said Holmes to himself.
"There is the tobacco shop, the little newspaper shop, the Coburg branch of the City and Suburban Bank, a vegetarian restaurant, and McFarlane's department store."
I tried to see London as I knew my friend was seeing London, but I knew I was missing subtle details.
"And now, Doctor," said Holmes, "our work is done, so it's time to have some fun.
A sandwich and a cup of coffee, and then off to violin-land, where all is sweetness and harmony, and where there are no red-headed clients to trouble us with their problems."
My friend is an enthusiastic music lover.
He enjoys playing the violin almost as much as he enjoys listening to others play.
We sat together in St. James' Hall, far removed from the mystery of the Red-Headed League.
Although I enjoyed the music, I couldn't stop myself from thinking that something quite unpleasant awaited the men Holmes was seeking.
My friend is a ruthless competitor and he takes the game very seriously.
After the concert, Holmes turned to me and said, "You, no doubt, want to go home, Doctor."
"Yes," I replied, "I would like to freshen up and have a pot of tea."
"Very well," said Holmes. "I still have some business to attend to, which will take several hours.
This affair at Coburg Square is quite critical."
"Why is that?" I asked.
"I believe a serious crime has been planned," replied Holmes, "but I have every reason to believe that we will be in time to stop it.
Today being Saturday makes things a little more complicated.
I'll want your help tonight, Doctor."
"What time?" I asked.
"I think ten this evening will be fine," said Holmes.
"I will meet you at Baker Street at ten," I replied.
I was in the process of hailing a carriage, when Holmes suddenly turned to me and said, "Doctor, there may be some risk tonight, so please put your army revolver in your pocket."
With a smile he turned, waved his hand, and disappeared almost instantly into the crowd.
If Holmes thought there might be danger, I knew that there was good reason for it, but I felt frustrated at not understanding why we might be in jeopardy.
The carriage ride home was joyless because I felt more stupid than usual.
I often suffer from these feelings when I am around Holmes.

I heard what he heard, I saw what he saw, and I imagine that I thought the way he had thought; however, whereas I had found no solution to our mystery, my friend not only understood what had happened, but also seemed to know what was about to happen.
I reviewed everything I knew about the Red-Headed League and our visit to Coburg Square, but found it futile.
The exercise produced more questions than answers:
Where were we going tonight? What kind of crime was going to be committed?
How would we stop it? Why was a revolver necessary?
The only question I thought I could answer was who.
I knew that the assistant was somehow involved, but my curiosity wouldn't be satisfied until that night.
I spent a restless evening at home and then started for Baker Street.
When I arrived, I saw Holmes standing on the street with two men.
"Ah, Watson," he greeted me, looking at his watch.

"Perfectly punctual, as usual. I think you are acquainted with Mr. Jones, the inspector from Scotland Yard, and this is Mr. Merryweather, the vice president of the Coburg branch of the City and Suburban Bank.
They will be our companions in tonight's undertaking."
I nodded to both men and was surprised to find myself rather excited and impatient to embark on this perilous adventure.
I stood in front of Baker Street, trying to contain my excitement.
Next to me was Mr. Jones, the inspector from Scotland Yard.
Mr. Merryweather of the City and Suburban Bank was also standing nearby.
And of course, there was my friend Sherlock Holmes.
"We are hunting in couples again, Doctor," said the inspector, sensing my mood.
"Your friend is wonderful at starting the chase, but he always calls this old dog to help him catch his fox."
"I hope it doesn't end in a wild goose chase," added Mr. Merryweather pessimistically.
"You can be confident in Mr. Holmes," said the inspector.
"Although he has his own methods, and they tend to be theoretical and a bit unconventional, he is a first-rate detective.
He has facilitated our work on a couple of cases."
"If you say so, Mr. Jones," said the vice president.
"I'm just a little disappointed about missing my weekly card game.
It's the first Saturday night in 27 years that I have missed."
"I think you will find," said Holmes, "that you will play for much higher stakes tonight than ever before, and that you will find this game more exciting than any hand of cards.
Your stakes tonight, Mr. Merryweather, are a treasure of gold; and for you, Jones, it will be a chance to apprehend the top man on your most-wanted list."
"John Clay . . . murderer, thief, and master forger?
I can think of no other criminal in London that I would rather catch," stated the inspector wishfully.
"John Clay?" I asked.
The name sounded familiar, but I couldn't remember the details.
"Yes, my dear doctor," said the inspector.
"He is a remarkable man. His grandfather was a royal duke, and John himself has attended the finest schools, including Oxford.
He is quite shrewd. He can rob a bank in Scotland one week and help to build an orphanage in Cornwall the next.
We have followed his trail for years, but he always manages to stay just a couple of steps ahead of us."
"I hope to introduce you tonight. I believe him to be none other than Vincent Spaulding, Mr. Wilson's assistant," said Holmes, checking his watch.
"It is after ten; we should go."
Mr. Jones and Mr. Merryweather left in the first carriage, and Holmes and I followed in the second.
Holmes didn't say a word during the ride, and I respected his silence.
I knew that our lives might very well depend on the accuracy of his thoughts.
The night was foggy, and the gas-lit streets were empty and quiet.
Out the window of the carriage, I recognized the same street we had walked down earlier in the day.
We stopped in front of the Coburg branch of the City and Suburban Bank.
Mr. Merryweather took us into the building, down a flight of stairs to the cellar, through several locked iron gates, and down many dark passages.
"You are not vulnerable from above," observed Holmes after we passed through another iron gate.
"Nor from below," said Mr. Merryweather confidently, stomping on the floor with the heel of his shoe.
"Oh!" he exclaimed in surprise. "It sounds quite hollow."
"Please be quiet," said Holmes, irritated.
"You have just risked the success of this adventure.
Now stand over there and stay out of our way."
Mr. Merryweather looked injured but did as he was told, while Holmes took the lantern.
With a magnifying glass, the detective examined the floor.
When he was finished, he said, "We have about an hour. They won't attempt anything until they are sure Mr. Wilson is in bed.
But once he is asleep, they won't lose a minute because the sooner they do their work, the more time they will have to make their escape."
"What will they steal?" I asked, looking around at the unmarked crates and boxes.
"Gold," said the vice president, pointing to fifteen crates in the corner.
"Each crate contains two thousand French napoleons.
The business transaction they were originally acquired for fell through, and we have had no opportunity to transfer the money to a safer location."
Holmes took another look at his watch and said, "It is time, Mr. Merryweather.
Once we conceal ourselves behind the boxes and crates, put a screen over the lantern."
"These are resolute and daring men," continued Holmes.
"Although we will surprise them, they may still do us harm.
I urge everyone to be cautious and to make no unnecessary moves.
They have but one retreat, so I hope you have done what I asked, Jones."
"Yes," replied the inspector quietly. "There are two officers waiting outside Mr. Wilson's house."
"Excellent," said Holmes. "All the holes are stopped."
Holmes, Mr. Jones, and I took our positions behind various crates and boxes.
We waited in the dark and perceived nothing happening until we saw light coming from under the floor.
At first the light shone through a single crack in the concrete, but over time the floor began to fracture.
It began to resemble a spider's web. A hole suddenly appeared in the center of the web, and a hand thrust through.
After feeling around, the hand withdrew under the floor, and the hole began to widen.
A clean-shaven man with a boyish face began to squeeze through the larger opening.
"It's all clear," said the man, oblivious to our presence. Soon another man, a redhead, also came up from below.
"Got you," said Holmes when Mr. Merryweather opened the shutter on the lantern.
There was a moment of blindness as my eyes adjusted to the sudden light.
Holmes had seized Clay by the collar, and Jones had grabbed the red-headed man by the shirt and said with a snicker, "Hello, there, ‘Mr. Ross.'"
Unfortunately the shirt ripped, and the man dived back down the hole.
Clay pulled a revolver out of his pocket, but before he could point it at anyone, Holmes used his walking stick to knock it to the floor.
"It's no use, Clay," said Holmes to the trapped man.
"As for your friend, there are men waiting for him at the door."
"I must compliment you," said Clay. "You seem to have prepared for every possibility."
"And I must compliment you," said Holmes.
"The idea of the Red-Headed League was quite original and ingenious."
While Inspector Jones handcuffed Clay and took him away, Holmes turned to the banker and said, "My expenses on this case have been slight, but I expect that the bank will happily reimburse them."
"Certainly, and a reward, if you like," said Mr. Merryweather.
"A reward won't be necessary," said Holmes.
"The experience was gratifying enough."
On the way back to Baker Street, I asked Holmes, "How did you know?"
"It was perfectly obvious," he explained.
"The purpose of that advertisement was to get Mr. Wilson out of his house for a certain number of hours each day.
When I saw the assistant's pants, I remembered his fondness for photography and disappearing into the cellar, and I began to suspect that he was tunneling.
When I saw the bank, I knew where he was tunneling to.
It was all quite elementary, my dear Watson."
Holmes and I were discussing some matters of importance when our deliberations were interrupted by Thorneycroft Huxtable, the headmaster of the Priory School.
He was a large man who filled the room.
He was usually dignified so his initial behavior was rather shocking.
Instead of presenting himself to us, he staggered against the table and then fell to the floor.
Holmes and I sprung to our feet.
Holmes grabbed a cushion for his head and I brought a glass of brandy to put to his lips.
His unshaven face, his uncombed hair, and the grime on his clothes told us that he had traveled far and that he had left in a hurry.
"What's wrong?" asked Holmes.
"Exhaustion; perhaps hunger and fatigue," I replied with my fingers on his pulse.
"Ah, a train ticket from Mackleton in the north of England," said Holmes as he drew the watch from his pocket.
"It's not even twelve o'clock. He certainly started early this morning."
Suddenly his eyes opened, the man scrambled to his feet, and his face flushed red with shame.
"Forgive this weakness, Mr. Holmes," said the man gravely.
"I am suffering from quite a bit of stress; this is what I would like to speak about."
"When you feel better . . ." began Holmes.
"I am quite ready now," interrupted the headmaster.
"We must be ready to leave soon, if we want to catch the next train back to Mackleton."
Holmes looked at the headmaster and said, "I do not know the nature of your case, but we are currently retained in several other cases.
Only something important . . ."
"Important!" shouted the headmaster.
"Of course it's important.
The only son of the Duke of Holdernesse has been kidnapped.
He is the wealthiest and perhaps greatest man I know.
Furthermore, he has authorized me to offer up to ten thousand pounds to anyone who can find his son or name the kidnappers."
"That's a generous offer," said Holmes.
"Watson, I think we might just accompany Dr. Huxtable to the north.
But first I must insist that you eat, and then tell us in detail what happened."
After a quick breakfast, the headmaster began his story.
He said that the duke's son was a recent arrival at the school.
The young lord had only arrived on the first of May, the beginning of the summer term.
He had been brought to the school by the duke's secretary, James Wilder.
Although he thought the ten-year-old Lord Saltire was a fine boy, it was obvious to the headmaster that the boy had not been entirely happy at home.
The cause of this unhappiness, according to the headmaster, was the duke's marriage.
The duke and the duchess had separated, and she now lived in France.
Finally, the headmaster concluded his introduction by stating that the boy had gone missing the night of the thirteenth of May.
Holmes asked some questions and we learned that the boy's room was located on the second floor, and that the boy had left through his window and climbed down a stout vine.
His disappearance was noted the following morning at seven.
A search of his room revealed that the boy had slept in his bed and that he had left fully dressed.
The room showed no signs of a struggle, so it seems that the boy had perhaps known his kidnapper.

Soon after discovering the boy's disappearance, the headmaster learned that the German teacher and his bicycle were also missing; an inspection of the teacher's room had revealed that he had only been partially dressed.
Holmes wrote several things in his notebook, looked at the headmaster and said, "You should have come to me sooner."
"It's not my fault," replied the headmaster.
"The duke wants to avoid a scandal."
"Has there been no official investigation then?" asked Holmes.
"There has, but it's been most disappointing," answered the headmaster.
"What are their theories?" asked Holmes.
The headmaster said that the police thought the German teacher's missing bicycle was a trick, and that they had left by some other means, and that's why the police were looking for them in Liverpool.
Holmes didn't think that theory seemed plausible, since the hidden bike had not been found.
Holmes was also suspicious of the police's belief that the German teacher was necessarily involved, since the boy had had no previous contact with this man.
"Did the boy have any visitors before his disappearance?" asked Holmes.
"No, but he did receive a letter," answered the headmaster. "But it was from his father."
"Did you read it?" asked Holmes.
"It is not our policy," said the headmaster.
"How do you know it was from his father?" asked Holmes.
"The duke's seal appeared on the outside," said the headmaster.
"How was the boy's relationship with his father? Were they friendly?" asked Holmes.
"The duke isn't friendly with anyone," replied the headmaster. "But he was always kind to the boy."
"The boy was closer to his mother, then?" asked Holmes.
"Yes," answered the headmaster. "That's what the duke's secretary had said."
"Dr. Huxtable," said Holmes. "If we are going to catch that train, I think it is time for us to go."
"Yes, quite right," said the headmaster.
"There is a cab waiting."
The train ride north was unremarkable, but the investigation heated up as soon as we arrived at the headmaster's school.
The doorman greeted the headmaster frantically, and informed us that the duke and his secretary, Mr. Wilder, were here, and waiting for the headmaster's return.
The duke and his secretary were waiting in Dr. Huxtable's study.
Both were standing. The duke was tall and well dressed.
A smaller, younger man stood next to him. I assumed it was his secretary.
He was a nervous man but he spoke in an authoritative manner and our interview began.
The duke's secretary spoke immediately after the introductions.
"I called this morning to prevent you from going to London. It seems I was too late.
His Grace is surprised that you have taken such steps without his consultation."
"When I learned the police had failed . . ." began the headmaster.
"His Grace is not convinced that they have," interrupted the secretary.
The headmaster tried to plead his case, but the secretary kept insisting that the duke was extremely displeased.
Finally the headmaster said, "There is a solution; Mr. Holmes can return on the train tomorrow."
"Hardly," said Holmes in his laziest voice.
"I think I'll hike your moors.
The only question is: will you allow us to stay here or shall we take a room at the village inn?"
The unfortunate headmaster looked as if he was about to jump off a cliff, when the duke's deep voice said, "I agree with Mr. Wilder, that you should have consulted with me.
But, since Mr. Holmes seems interested in the case whether he is wanted here or not, he ought to stay with me at Holdernesse Hall."
"I thank your Grace," said Holmes humbly.
"But for the purposes of my investigation, I should remain here at the school."
"As you like," responded the duke.
"My secretary and I are happy to provide you with any information."
"I may need to speak with you at the Hall," said Holmes.
"For now, however, I was just wondering whether you have made up any explanation for the disappearance of your son?"
"I have not," said the duke.
"Sorry, if this is uncomfortable, but I have to know: do you think the duchess had anything to do with it?" asked Holmes politely.
The duke hesitated, and then replied, "I do not think so."
"The other obvious explanation is kidnapping for ransom," continued Holmes.
"Have you received any kind of ransom demand?"
"No," said the duke.
"Last question, your Grace," said Holmes. "I know you wrote to your son on the last day of his disappearance. Was there anything in the letter that may have upset him?"
"No, certainly not," said the duke abruptly.
"Did you post the letter yourself?" continued Holmes.
The answer to Holmes' question came not from the duke but from his secretary.
"His Grace does not post his own letters," said the secretary angrily.
"I post all his letters."
"Are you sure you posted the one in question?" asked Holmes.
"Yes," replied the secretary. "I observed it."
"How many letters does your Grace usually write each day?" asked Holmes.
"Twenty to thirty," answered the duke.
"But surely this is irrelevant. I have advised the police to continue their search in the south of France.
Although I do not think my wife is involved, the boy may have had some wrongheaded notion—no doubt aided by that German teacher.
If you discover anything, Mr. Holmes, contact me at the Hall."
It seemed Holmes had more questions, but the duke's abrupt manner ended the interview.
The doorman had barely closed the door after the duke and his secretary, when Holmes energetically began his investigation.
Holmes searched the rooms of the boy and the German teacher, but they revealed nothing further.
Next Holmes left the school and came back an hour later with a large map of the local area.
"Watson, geography is the key to this mystery," said Holmes.
I helped him lay the map out, and then we began to examine it.
Holmes put a colored pin into the map where the Priory School was located.
"Look here," said Holmes.
"Here's the main road running east and west past the school.
Please note that there is no side road for a mile either way.
If they went by road, it had to be this road."
Holmes then said he doubted if they had taken the road.
After he had obtained the map, he had talked to a constable on duty near the eastern side road.
The constable swore that he had seen no one that night, and Holmes commented that he was a very reliable witness.
Holmes' second conversation had been with the landlady of the Red Bull inn.
On the night in question, she had been ill and so she had sent for the doctor.
Her son had waited for the doctor until morning, and the boy had sworn he saw no one on the road all night.
If the combined testimonies were accurate, it meant the fugitives had not taken the road.
I thought the testimonies to be reliable, so I agreed with Holmes' deductions.
"These testimonies suggest that a different route was taken," said Holmes.
"But the bicycle," I said.
"A good cyclist doesn't need a road," said Holmes.
"Besides, the moor is intersected with paths, and the moon was full."
Suddenly there was an agitated knock on our door, and the door burst open.
"At last we have a clue," exclaimed the headmaster.
"The boy's cap has been found with a bunch of Gypsies who had been camping on the moor.
They say they found it on the moor, but the police are not convinced.
I guess we're not going to need your services after all."
Holmes acknowledged that finding the cap was indeed good news, but he didn't think the Gypsies were involved.
The headmaster assured us that the police had it under control.
The next morning, Holmes and I started out early.
Holmes said we should head toward the area of the moor that was marshy, because there may be tracks there.
For most of the morning, the only tracks we found were those of sheep and cows, but then at midday we came to something that was certainly a bicycle track.
I shouted for joy, but Homes calmed me.
"Indeed a bicycle tire, but not the German teacher's bicycle.
These tire tracks are made by a patched set of Dunlop tires; the bicycle we want has Palmer tires."
I wondered if it was the boy's bicycle, but Holmes seemed to think not.
Nonetheless, he was curious so we decided to follow the bicycle tracks back in the direction of the school.
The path of the patched Dunlop tires led us back in the direction of the school.
Although we lost sight of the tire tracks from time to time, we usually regained it after a while.
Whenever we sighted the tire tracks, they were almost always seen alongside the hooves of cows.
The tracks took us to the Ragged Shaw, a small wooded area that was behind the school.
"Well," said Holmes, "this is an interesting complication.
It seems that this cyclist must have emerged from these woods, because the path begins and ends here."
Holmes thoughtfully took his pipe out of his pocket and had a smoke.
After his smoke Holmes continued, "It is, of course, possible that a cunning man might change the tires on his bicycle."
I nodded in agreement.
"A criminal capable of such a plan," continued Holmes, "is a man I should be proud to do business with.
But enough of this speculation, we have still a lot to explore."
Holmes led me to another muddy portion of the moor, and it was here that Holmes became truly excited.
In the mud there were the tracks of Palmer tires.
"Here is the German teacher," said Holmes happily.
"So far our reasoning has been sound, so let's follow the tracks . . . though I fear they won't lead very far."
Once again we did our best to follow the scattered tracks.
At one such interval, Holmes stopped and observed that the cyclist was sprinting, because his weight had been moved to the front wheel as if he was leaning over the handlebars.
"Look, here!" exclaimed Holmes. "He has fallen."
To the side of the path, there was a flattened area of bushes that had been made by the fall of the rider.
On closer examination, we found that some of the bushes were covered in blood.
"Stand clear, Watson," said Holmes. "We must read this very carefully.
He fell wounded, because the blood is not where his legs or arms would have made contact with the ground."
"Was he attacked by a bull?" I asked.
"There are cow hoof marks on the ground."
"Unlikely," said Holmes. "But you are right to note the cow hoofs.
There are no other tracks to explain this freakish event.
It seems he remounted his bicycle; let us continue."
We had not gone far when the gleam of metal flickered from among the bushes and grass.
We hurried to the spot where we found a Palmer-tired bicycle covered in blood.
Not far from the bicycle lay a tall, bearded man on his side.
I knew in an instant he must be dead.
Holmes and I carefully turned him over to examine him, and that's when we discovered the horrible blow to his skull.
We had no doubt we had found the German teacher, but I could tell that Holmes was troubled by our discovery.
"It's a bit difficult to decide what to do," said Holmes.
"I want to continue, because the young duke may be in danger, but, on the other hand, we must inform the police of our startling discovery."
"I could take a note back," I offered.
"No, Watson, I need . . ." Suddenly Holmes stopped talking and listened very intently.
"Do you hear that, Watson?" asked Holmes.
"I believe there is a man working behind that small hill. Ask him over, won't you?"
I brought the man, and Holmes sent him with a note to the headmaster.
Holmes took out his pipe and reviewed the facts: first, the boy had left on his own free will;
second, the German teacher had followed the boy; third, the boy had had a companion strong enough to kill the German teacher;
and fourth, we had found the German teacher five miles from the school, which meant the boy and his companion had had a fairly swift means of traveling.
"Well," said Holmes, "we aren't any nearer to a solution, but we have followed one set of tracks to their end.
Let us now see about those patched Dunlop tires."
We picked up the tracks of the Dunlop bicycle tires, and followed them away from the school.
The tracks led to a high bushy hill. On the top of the hill the path forked.
One path lead in the direction of Holderness Hall and the other led toward a village, but there were no tire tracks to help us decide which way the rider had gone.
Holmes decided to take the path toward the village.
As we approached the village inn, Holmes stumbled, groaned, and grabbed his ankle.
"Give me your shoulder, Watson," said Holmes. I supported my friend and led him toward the inn.
An elderly man sat near the front of the inn smoking his pipe, and Holmes greeted him.
"How are you, Mr. Reuben Hayes?"
The man was a bit surprised, and asked suspiciously, "Who are you and how do you know my name?"
"It's printed on the sign above your head," said Holmes.
"Do you, perhaps, have a carriage in your stable?"
"No," said the man coldly.
"I've sprained my ankle," explained Holmes. "I can barely walk."
"So hop," said the man ungraciously.
The man was obviously hostile, but Holmes continued to ask him questions.
Holmes asked about a bicycle, but he had none.
Holmes mentioned that the police had been informed about the duke's son, and the man became agitated.
He asked about the news, and Holmes said there had been a telegram from Liverpool.
The man seemed to relax.
He then informed us that he had once worked for the duke, but had been fired.
Holmes sympathized with him, and said, "I understand your hard feelings, but can you help me get to the Hall?"
"Aye, my two horses can take you to the Hall.
I hate the duke, but I bear no ill feeling toward his son.
I am glad he's safe in Liverpool."
"Before we go, we'll have some dinner," said Holmes. The man took Holmes' money and left.
Once the man had left, I was amazed at Holmes' quick recovery. His ankle showed no sign of being sprained.
"Come, Watson. There is much for us to discover here.
This man is certainly more than he seems. We need to take a look at those horses he mentioned."
We hurried out into the inn's courtyard.
Holmes was quite excited and exclaimed, "By heavens, Watson, I think I've got it.
Do you remember all those cow tracks we saw today?"
"Yes," I answered, perplexed. "They were everywhere."
"Exactly. How many cows did you see on the moor today?" Holmes asked, smiling.
"None," I said, not understanding.
"Doesn't this seem strange?" continued Holmes.
"Yes," I agreed.
"Think about those tracks for a moment, Watson," said Holmes as he began to draw in the dirt.
"Some looked like this: : : : : : : : others like this: : : : : : : and occasionally like this: : : : What does this suggest to you?"
I shook my head and said, "Nothing, but I believe it means something to you."
"Indeed," said Holmes.
"The cow must be quite remarkable because it can walk, canter and gallop, and I have never met a cow like that."
Holmes and I slipped into the stable unnoticed.
Holmes immediately went to the horses and raised one of their legs.
Holmes laughed out loud and said, "The horses have old horseshoes, but they have been put on very recently."
I wanted to ask Holmes to explain, but before I could, an extremely angry Mr. Hayes burst into the stable holding a short, metal-headed stick.
"Spies! What are you doing here!" he screamed.
I was glad that I had my revolver in my pocket, because he walked toward us with murder in his eyes.
"Why, Mr. Hayes," said Holmes coolly. "You act as if you have something to hide."
The man mastered his emotions with a supreme effort of will, and said with a fake laugh, "Poke around as you like, you will find nothing here.
Once you've had a look, you had better leave at once."
"We've had a look," said Holmes.
"And my ankle is feeling better. Perhaps we'll walk back to the Hall."
"The road's over there," said Mr. Hayes, waving his menacing stick.
The man watched us leave. We had walked along the road for only about five minutes when Holmes suddenly stopped.
"I think we need to return to the inn," said Holmes. "There's one more piece to this puzzle.
I need to find it before we see the duke."
I looked at Holmes and said, "That Mr. Hayes is a villain. I'm sure of it."
"Watson! Quick! Off the road!" whispered Holmes urgently.
A cyclist was coming quickly down the road from Holdernesse Hall, and Holmes and I had only a moment to hide ourselves.
We watched as the cyclist passed in a cloud of dust.
When he had passed I let out a soft whistle and Holmes exclaimed, "It was Mr. Wilder, the duke's secretary; our plot thickens.
Come! Let us return to the inn."
As night fell, we carefully made our way back to the inn, and hid.
The courtyard appeared deserted. Wilder's bicycle rested against the wall, but we could hear sounds coming from the stable.
A moment later we heard the clatter of hooves and the rattle of a cart moving at a furious pace.
"What do you make of that?" I asked Holmes.
"One man fleeing in a cart," replied Holmes.
"But it wasn't Mr. Wilder, because there he is at the window. He seems to be expecting someone."
A second figure appeared on the road five minutes later, and the secretary opened the door.
"Curious," said Holmes. "Come, we must have a look into the inn."
Holmes used my back to climb up and peek in the window.
He was hardly up before he was down again. "Come, my friend. Our work is nearly done. We need to get back to the school.
I think by tomorrow evening we'll be returning to London."
When I awoke the following morning, Holmes was gone, so I occupied myself with the newspaper.
Holmes returned by mid-morning, and said, "It's time for us to pay a visit to Holdernesse Hall."
On our arrival we were greeted by a very nervous Mr. Wilder, who was obviously not pleased to see us.
"If you have come to see the duke, I am afraid it will have to wait. The duke is sick."
"Sick or not, I will see the duke!" insisted Holmes, who simply would not accept no for an answer.
An hour later, Mr. Wilder led us into the duke's study.
"Your Grace," said Holmes formally, "I believe my business with you should be conducted in the absence of your secretary."
Mr. Wilder turned very pale, and appeared about to protest when the duke dismissed him.
After Mr. Wilder had left, Holmes asked, "Is it true you offered a reward for this case?"
The duke nodded.
Holmes continued, "Ten thousand pounds—five for anyone who could name the whereabouts of your son, and another five for the names of the people involved."
Again the duke nodded. "Excellent," said Holmes.
"Please write me a check for ten thousand pounds."
The duke stood up and glared at Holmes. "Is this a joke?"
"Not at all, Your Grace," said Holmes. "Your son is at the Fighting Cock Inn, and . . ."
"And . . . and who do you accuse?" interrupted the anxious duke.
"I accuse YOU," said Holmes firmly.
The duke sat down with his head down and wrote the check.
"I will make the check out for 12,000 pounds," said the duke, "if you will kindly forget this whole incident."
Holmes shook his head. "Too late for that, Your Grace, the murderer of the schoolteacher has already been arrested."
"I see," said the duke. "Then it is time for a complete confession."
The duke explained how Mr. Wilder was his illegitimate son, and how he was jealous of the young lord.
The young lord had been sent to the Priory School for fear of his safety.
Mr. Wilder kidnapped the young lord in order to blackmail the duke, but the German teacher had seen them leave.
Mr. Wilder and the young lord had left the school in a cart, driven by the innkeeper. The German teacher had followed them.
The innkeeper, worried about getting caught, had hit the schoolteacher with his club.
Unfortunately the German teacher had died from his injuries.
Holmes and I had not spotted the hooves of the horse and carriage because the innkeeper had cleverly changed the horseshoes, and made them look like cows' hooves.
Holmes scolded the duke, and the duke accepted the scolding quietly.
That evening as Holmes and I boarded our London-bound train, Holmes chuckled and said, "A most satisfactory ending to a sordid family affair.
I believe our duke will be a much better father to both sons, and we, my dear friend, are a great deal richer."
When I reflect on the last eight years and the seventy cases in which I have been involved, none seem as sinister or as strange as that of the speckled band.
Of course I cannot take the credit for solving the mystery; that claim belongs to my friend and associate, the famous detective Mr. Sherlock Holmes.
It was during the early spring of 1883 when I awoke one morning to find Holmes standing over my bed in the apartment we shared at 221B Baker Street.
"Watson, we have a new client!" he announced. "She is downstairs and seems to be quite upset.
Get dressed and join us—oh, and bring your notebook. This looks as if it may be our most interesting case yet."
"My dear fellow," I responded, "I would not miss it for anything."
I quickly pulled on my trousers and buttoned up my shirt.
In my haste I forgot to comb my hair, but I did remember to grab my favorite leather notebook.
I hustled down the stairs to the sitting room.
Standing close to the fireplace was a young woman of about thirty who appeared agitated.
Her expression was tired and haggard, and a streak of gray ran through her hair.
"Thanks for joining us, Watson," Holmes said.
"This is Lady Helen Stoner. She arrived by carriage this morning to seek our assistance with an unusual situation."
"Although I don't even know for sure," Miss Stoner added quickly, "whether a crime has been committed."
"Well, if you would explain to Dr. Watson here what you have just told me, I believe we will all agree that there is, indeed, a mystery to be solved."
"Of course," she began, with a slight tremble in her voice.
"I am the stepdaughter of Dr. Grimesby Roylott, the last surviving heir to one of the oldest Saxon families in England.
My mother was a young widow when she met the doctor in India.
He had a successful medical practice there.
Dr. Roylott agreed to marry her in exchange for her monthly pension—you see, my father was highly ranked in the military and left us with a hefty sum upon his death."
At this Holmes gave a slight nod of understanding.
Taking notice, Miss Stoner cut in. "Let me correct any misunderstanding if one exists, Mr. Holmes.
Dr. Roylott was kind and caring to both my twin sister, Julia, and me. We were only two years old at the time.
We lived together happily for the next few years until an incident forced us to return to England."
"Would you explain this ‘incident,' Miss Stoner?" said Holmes.
"My stepfather was a professional gentleman, but he did have a temper.
When he discovered that one of our servants had been stealing food from the cupboards, he flew into a fit of rage and killed him on the spot.
Fearing that he would be imprisoned, we fled the country and returned to his ancestral home near Waterloo."
"The mansion called Stoke Moran?" Holmes inquired.
"Yes, it has been in the family for generations.
The mansion was not in good condition when we moved in, but we made it into a home.
In fact, we were content for a long time until my mother died.
She was killed in a railway accident eight years after our return."
"I imagine this had a profound effect on your family?" Holmes asked.
"It did," Miss Stoner responded, lowering her eyes to the floor.
"Not only did we lose our mother, but upon her death, our kindhearted stepfather ceased to practice medicine and began to exhibit bizarre behavior.
He locked himself in the house and rarely went out. When he did, he often ended up in heated arguments with the neighbors.
It was terrible! He was even brought back to the house once by the police after he started a brawl in the nearby village.
But that's not all, Mr. Holmes. Since he no longer worked, Stoke Moran began to decay even more.
Julia and I attempted to keep the house up, but it was no use.
What's worse, we could not keep any servants. They quit as soon as they saw the baboon and the cheetah—"
"Baboon and cheetah?" I interjected.
"Yes, my stepfather has a passion for exotic animals.
He frequently imports them from India and allows them to run wild in the yard. It's awful! But that's not all.
A few years ago, he invited Gypsies to live on our land. They have pitched their tents in the woods behind the house.
The situation became so stressful that Julia's hair was already turning white before she died."
"Your sister is dead then?" Holmes asked.
I am always so impressed by Holmes' sensitivity in these delicate matters.
Miss Stoner paused and put down the teacup she was holding.
Then, after several moments, she said, "Julia died two years ago, and this is the mystery that I beg you to solve."
"Watson, are you writing all of this down?" Holmes motioned to my leather notebook.
I nodded and gestured to Miss Stoner to continue her story.
"Julia was engaged to be married. She had informed us of her plans during a family dinner at Stoke Moran.
Dr. Roylott was thrilled and insisted that the wedding be held in the local parish.
But it was never to be. The night before the wedding, Julia came to my room just after midnight.
‘Helen,' she said, ‘may I ask you a question?' ‘Of course,' I replied.
‘Do you hear whistling at night?' she said.
I had had no similar experience and told her so.
"She looked at me strangely and inquired, ‘Do you think it might be the Gypsies at the windows?'
‘No,' I responded. ‘If that were true, then I would hear it too.'
‘Maybe it's the baboon or the cheetah then?'
‘I don't think so,' I answered. But I had no other explanation to offer."
Holmes leaned forward, a gesture I knew indicated that the young woman's story was of great interest to him.
"Please . . . ," he said, urging her on.
"After our talk Julia excused herself and then went to bed.
I did the same, but I was quite concerned for her.
After tossing and turning for over an hour, I finally fell into a deep sleep until I was startled awake by the sound of Julia screaming.
I burst out of bed and ran down the corridor toward her room.
I heard the whistling sound and a clang of metal as a shiver of terror ran through my body.
When I arrived at her door, I found it unlocked—we usually keep them locked for fear that an animal may wander into the house at night.
Inside, my poor sister lay writhing in pain on the floor.
I rushed to her side and held her in my arms, but nothing I did would ease her horrible pain.
Then she said something that I will never forget.
"She looked up into my eyes and, with considerable effort, gasped, ‘Oh my God, Helen!
It was the speckled band!' I sent for medical aid, but my dear sister was dead."
The sun was just beginning to peek into the windows of our apartment at 221B Baker Street when the lady of Stoke Moran finished her terrible story about the death of her twin sister.
"If I may," my friend and associate Mr. Sherlock Holmes asked, "I would like to make sure of some of the details before I begin my investigation.
Now, you mentioned there was a whistling sound followed by a clang of metal. Are you sure this is what you heard that night?"
"I will never forget it," responded Miss Stoner.
"It was an odd whistle that sounded like a strange melody, followed by a harsh metallic clang."
"Did you explain these events to the coroner?" inquired Holmes.
"Of course, but even after a thorough examination of her body, he was still unable to determine the cause of death.
There were no signs of violence and no evidence of poison.
Mr. Holmes, you may think I am silly, but I believe that my sister died of fright.
She was white as a ghost when I found her. Something terrible must have roused her from her bed."
It was then that I remembered the guests in the woods behind the house and spoke up.
"Do you think it was the Gypsies?" I asked.
Miss Stoner nodded. "The Gypsy women often wear handkerchiefs over their hair.
Perhaps this is what Julia meant by ‘the speckled band.'"
I wrote down this evidence in my leather notebook and glanced over at Holmes, who was now sitting with his head tilted back and his eyes closed.
He did this only when he was deep in thought.
"What is the situation at Stoke Moran now?" I asked, hoping this would encourage Miss Stoner to reveal more facts about the case.
"That is why I am here," explained the young woman.
Holmes appeared to perk up at this statement and opened his eyes. "Continue, please," he said.
Miss Stoner avoided eye contact with Holmes. Instead she stared sadly down at the floor.
She became slightly more agitated, and a shudder of terror seemed to ripple through her before she spoke.
"As I told you," she said, "it's been two years since Julia's death.
Last summer, when I was the loneliest I have ever been, my dear friend Mr. Percy Armitage of Crane Water did me the honor of asking for my hand in marriage.
With no objection from my stepfather, I graciously accepted. The two of us plan to wed next month."
"Congratulations!" I interrupted. "You must be very happy."
"I would be," she explained, "except there have been some very frightful events."
At this comment Holmes leaned forward in a position I knew signaled great interest.
"Last week," Miss Stoner continued, "Dr. Roylott informed me that he would be making some renovations in the house.
He told me I would need to move from my own room at the end of the hall into Julia's old room, next to his own.
I was surprised to hear this—we have not done repairs in quite some time—but I moved my things as requested.
It has been awful trying to sleep in Julia's room!
I either lie awake all night or suffer horrible nightmares when I do manage to fall asleep.
Last evening, however, something terrifying happened.
I heard a whistling sound—the same one I remember from the night Julia died!
That is why I have contacted you, Mr. Holmes. I believe I am in grave danger."
"This is a serious case, Miss Stoner," Holmes agreed.
Then he pointed to her arms and said, "But you are also hiding something."
Miss Stoner moved her arms in a way that caused her sleeves to slip upward, revealing several large bruises on her forearms.
"Yes," she said.
"When I informed my stepfather that I was having trouble sleeping and wished to move out of Julia's room, he grabbed me hard and demanded that I stay until the repairs are complete.
Do you think that you can help me?"
Holmes immediately offered his assistance but explained to our new client that he would first need to gather a good deal of information.
He then asked if it would be possible for the two of us to examine the rooms at Stoke Moran without Dr. Roylott's knowledge.
"He will be out of the house today," Miss Stoner said.
"He is running errands in town and will not be home until after the supper hour."
Holmes made plans to meet the young woman at Stoke Moran that afternoon.
Appearing relieved to have acquired our help, she said good-bye and left.
"A most interesting case indeed," I said aloud.
Holmes, who had failed to nod in agreement, was already gathering his things to begin his research. "
Where are you going, my good fellow?" I asked, quite surprised that he was so hasty in his preparations.
"I have some research to complete before we travel to Stoke Moran," Holmes replied.
"Oh, but I suppose I should not assume that you will be joining me on the adventure. It will be dangerous."
"I most definitely will!" I responded without delay.
"But I simply cannot understand what is happening to Miss Stoner and what killed her dear sister. The evidence is confusing . . ."
I was hoping that Holmes would enlighten me.
But before he had a chance to respond, the front door to the apartment swung open wildly and a tall figure marched through.
In an angry voice, the stranger proclaimed, "I am Dr. Grimesby Roylott, and I have followed my stepdaughter to your apartment.
I demand to know who you two are!"
"This is my colleague, Dr. Watson, and I am Mr. Sherlock Holmes," answered my associate as he put out his hand to greet the unwelcome guest.
Roylott, however, ignored the polite gesture.
He moved quickly to the fireplace and picked up the metal poker that was lying on the mantel.
"The famous detective? Well, my good man, I don't want you meddling in my affairs," Roylott said threateningly.
Then, much to my surprise, he took the poker in both hands and, with incredible strength, bent it in half. "Do I make myself clear?"
Holmes did not respond. He merely pulled back his outstretched hand and placed it into the right pocket of his vest.
As he did this, I moved closer to him in case the situation erupted into a fight.
Holmes, of course, was a competent boxer; nevertheless, I wanted to show my loyalty to him.
I did not appreciate such bullying in our home.
My protection, however, wasn't necessary because Roylott quickly spun around and marched out the door with the same anger in his step as when he arrived.
I rushed over and bolted the door shut behind him.
"What a pleasant gentleman," said Holmes sarcastically.
Then he walked over to the fireplace, picked up the poker, and easily bent it back into shape.

He placed it back on the mantel, retrieved his briefcase from the bedroom, and announced, "I am going to the hospital library to do some research and will be back in time to meet with you before we leave for Stoke Moran.
Pack your bag, Watson, and don't forget to bring your pistol. It looks as if we may require it today."
I was just getting my things packed up when Holmes returned from his excursions.
I noticed that he was carrying a sheet of blue paper in his hand, but before I could ask him how his investigation had progressed, Holmes made an announcement.
"Watson," he said, "I have uncovered a very interesting set of facts.
First, I spoke with a physician at the hospital library about the mysterious death of Miss Julia Stoner.
Then, I paid a visit to city hall, where I reviewed the will of the deceased wife."
"Our client's mother?" I inquired.
"Yes, it seems that she left Dr. Roylott an income of almost 1,100 pounds; however, the sum has shrunk slightly over the years due to inflation.
Each daughter can claim an income of 250 pounds upon her marriage, which would leave the widower with very little.
Since he no longer practices medicine and is responsible for the care of the family estate, it is clear that he would end up in poverty in the event that his stepdaughters wed."
"This is definitely a motive for the crime, Holmes," I stated.
My friend and associate nodded in agreement and quickly gathered his things to prepare for our trip to Stoke Moran.
Then we left the house on Baker Street by cab and caught the afternoon train from Waterloo to Leatherhead, a small town several miles from the mansion.
At Leatherhead we hired a carriage to take us to the property.
Holmes spent the entire trip sitting with his arms folded in front of his chest and his hat pulled down over his eyes.
After several miles the driver shouted out, "It's over there, sirs, just beyond the village."
Holmes immediately sat upright and adjusted his hat.
About a mile to the east was a rolling hill covered in a thick grove of trees through which the peak of a gray rooftop was visible.
"Stoke Moran?" Holmes asked.
"Yes, the home of Dr. Grimesby Roylott, sir. I could take you around to the front door if you'd like.
But it's faster if I drop you here and you walk in along the footpath.
I believe that's Miss Stoner walking there right now."
Holmes paid the fare, and the two of us climbed out of the carriage.
Miss Stoner hurried over to greet us. "I have been eagerly awaiting your arrival," she said.
"Dr. Roylott should be gone for the rest of the day."
"Yes," replied Holmes. "We have had the pleasure of making the doctor's acquaintance."
"Oh, good heavens!" Miss Stoner exclaimed with great surprise.
"Has he followed me then? I never know when I am safe from him. What will I say when he returns?"
"Your safety is our greatest concern," Holmes said consolingly.
"You must keep your door locked tonight. If he becomes violent, is there somewhere you can go?"
"I have an aunt in the village," said Miss Stoner.
"If need be," said Holmes, "we'll take you there."
Miss Stoner seemed quite relieved by this, but she continued to talk about her fears as we walked across the field toward the house.
As we neared the property, I noticed that it was quite old and run-down.
Some of the windows and doors were covered with wooden boards.
The mansion's gray bricks were covered in thick moss, and part of the roof had caved in.
The central portion, however, was more modern, and a curl of blue smoke escaped from the chimney.
"There are shutters on the windows," Holmes observed.
"Yes, I bar them shut every night before bed to keep the animals out," explained Miss Stoner.
Holmes strolled over to the windows and examined them carefully.
"There doesn't seem to be any way to break in from the outside," he said.
"That would likely rule out any involvement by the Gypsies.
Now, did you say that your stepfather was doing some renovations?"
"Yes, but no work has been done so far. I fear it's just an excuse to get me to change rooms."
Holmes continued to examine the physical structure of the house as we walked through the front door and down the hallway.
I noticed three doors along the left-hand side.
"Where is your room?" Holmes asked our client.
"My room is at the end of the hall," she responded. "Follow me."
Miss Stoner's room was cold and rather shabby, but otherwise ordinary.
There was nothing to note, so we quickly moved into the middle room.
"This one belonged to Julia," she explained. "But I have moved my things in here now."
"This is odd," said Holmes. He took his magnifying glass out of his coat pocket and began to examine the floor.
"The bed is bolted to the floor, preventing it from being moved to another location.
Hmm . . . here is also a bell rope hanging down from the ceiling to the bed.
Didn't you say you had no servants?"
"Yes, that is correct. We haven't had a servant in several months."
Holmes pulled the cord and announced, "Why, it's a fake! It doesn't ring at all.
Interesting . . . Look up here, Watson, near the ceiling.
There is a small square window through the wall connecting this room to the one next to it.
I would guess that it could be part of the ventilation system—you see, there is a metal door that can be closed to keep out the cold air—but it doesn't seem to be connected to the outside.
I wonder what it could be for?"
"I don't know," Miss Stoner said, sounding increasingly worried.
"It was put in about three years ago. The room next door is Dr. Roylott's."
At this announcement Holmes raised his eyebrows and nodded his head.
I was sure that he had deduced something important from the evidence—something that I could not figure out on my own.
Holmes could often see answers where others could not.
When Holmes was finished examining Julia's room, we moved into Dr. Roylott's room to complete our investigation.
There we discovered a filing cabinet, a single bed, and other regular items that one would expect to find in a bedroom.
Holmes, however, spent a long time examining an old wooden chair that sat beside the bed.
He also made several unusual observations.
"There is a saucer of milk on the floor," he noted. "Miss Stoner, do you have a cat?"
"No, we do not," she replied.
"Could it be for the cheetah?" I asked.
"I don't think so," said Holmes.
"It would be too small to satisfy a beast that big. Look here," he said, pointing to the head of the bed.
Hanging from the bedpost was what looked like a dog's leash that had been curled up at the end into a loop.
"I'm getting quite concerned. I fear any man who uses his intelligence for evil deeds."
Holmes' comment sent a shiver up my spine.
For the first time, I began to realize how much danger we were actually in.
Thank goodness I had remembered to put my pistol in my bag.
"Miss Stoner," Holmes said in a soft, reassuring voice, "tonight you must prepare for bed as usual.
But do not sleep. Instead I want you to wait until you hear Dr. Roylott prepare for bed.
When you think he is asleep, I want you to place your lantern in Julia's open window and escape to your own room down the hall.
Don't forget to lock your doors and bar your shutters. We will be watching from the village.
When we see your lantern, we will sneak through Julia's window and spend the night in the room.
Now let's go, Watson. We will take a room at the inn and wait for the signal.
I hope that tonight we will be able to solve this mystery!"
I accompanied Holmes to the village inn, and we arranged for a room from which we could see Julia's window at Stoke Moran.
While we waited for the lantern signal, Holmes asked me to assist him with a review of the facts.
"Well, there seemed to be nothing strange about Miss Stoner's room," I began.
"But her sister Julia's room did seem a bit odd.
First of all, the bed was bolted to the floor, which prevented it from being moved.
Then, of course, there was the bell rope—it didn't even work!
And, from what Miss Stoner has told us, there would be no use for it anyway.
Also, there was the ventilation window that linked her room to Dr. Roylott's."
"I think that's everything, Watson," said Holmes. "Now, what about Roylott's room?"
"Two things are puzzling," I replied, "the saucer of milk on the floor and the dog's leash hanging from the bedpost."
"Indeed," said Holmes.
For several hours I sat in the armchair by the window, keeping watch for the signal as Holmes reclined on the bed with his hat tipped over his eyes.
Finally he broke the silence.
"It's going to be a dangerous night, my dear Watson," he said. "If you wish to return to the safety of London, I will not hold it against you."
"I will be at your side, Holmes!" I quickly responded.
"I only wish that I could deduce more from the clues. I hate to admit it, but I don't really know what's happening."
Holmes gave me a kind smile.
"Watson," he said, "you are a trustworthy man, a fine friend, and an excellent associate. I knew I could count on you."
Just after midnight I spotted the lantern and alerted Holmes.
As he prepared his things, I slipped my pistol into the inside pocket of my suit jacket, and we left the inn.
We walked along the pathway toward the window of Julia's room, which had been left open for us.
I was just about to give Holmes a boost up to the window when I noticed a hideous figure moving in the shadows.
"Oh my! What was that?" I whispered, trying hard not to appear frightened.
"It's the baboon!" replied Holmes. "It gave me quite a fright as well."
We looked at each other and laughed softly.
Then, quietly, we climbed through the window and into the room.
"It may be a while before anything occurs," advised Holmes. "Why don't you sit in the chair and get comfortable?"
Without an explanation Holmes then placed a pack of matches next to the candles on the bedside table and lay down on the bed, holding his cane close to his side.
I barely had a chance to ponder his actions before a gleam of light appeared through the ventilation window.
This was accompanied by the smell of burning oil and heated metal.
"Roylott has lit his lantern," Holmes whispered. "Be prepared."
There was no further action for another few minutes.
Then the silence was interrupted by an odd hissing sound much like that of a jet of steam escaping from a kettle.
When Holmes heard it, he immediately leaped from the bed, lit the candles, and then lashed the bed with his cane.
My heart was racing, but with all the shadows, I couldn't see what was happening.
I could tell, however, that Holmes was frightened. All the color had drained from his face.
Just then a piercing scream came from Roylott's room, and Holmes stopped.
"Is it over?" I asked frantically.
"I believe so," responded Holmes. "Follow me to the doctor's room."
We rushed toward Roylott's door, which luckily we discovered unlocked. Inside I was shocked to see the doctor lying face up on the floor.
His face was frozen in a look of absolute terror, and he was clearly dead.
Around his head was a speckled band—was this what had killed Julia too?
I was about to lean down to examine it when Holmes suddenly pulled me away.
Much to my surprise, the band moved! It was then that I realized the reason for Holmes' action.
It was a swamp adder, the most poisonous snake in India!
Holmes quickly stepped over the body, grabbed the leash from the bedpost, and snapped the looped end around the snake's neck.
Then he threw the serpent into the filing cabinet and closed the drawer, securing the snake inside. I gave a sigh of relief.
"Don't worry, Watson," Holmes said. "Go get Miss Stoner and let her know that we have solved her mystery."
The next morning, after the police had been called and the two of us had given our testimony, we caught the train home to London.
I took this opportunity to ask Holmes to tell me how he had known about the snake.
"Ah," he began. "I was initially confused by Miss Stoner's mention of the Gypsies.
But the more I began to research the case, the more it seemed unfair to blame the crime on them.
It was obvious that Dr. Roylott had the only motive for committing the murder.
At the hospital library, I learned that snake venom might also cause its victim to die without any visible sign—I have always been fascinated by toxicology!
I suspected a snake could be the culprit after Miss Stoner mentioned Roylott's love of exotic animals.
Of course, when we discovered the ventilation window that connected Roylott's room to Julia's, I was convinced a snake was the murder weapon.
I knew that serpents do not like fire, which is why I brought the pack of matches with us to the room and lit the candle."
"I see!" I exclaimed. "But what about the other clues? The bell rope, for example?"
"The bell rope worked like a bridge between the ventilation window and the bed.
Roylott must have trained the snake to climb through the ventilation window and down the bell rope onto the bed, which, you will recall, was bolted to the floor.
The snake must have done this for several nights without attacking, but eventually it did and poor Julia was bitten."
"How do you explain the whistling sound and the metal clang that Miss Stoner reported?" I asked.
"We didn't hear either last night."
Holmes gave me a big smile and said, "Aha! I believe that the doctor had trained the snake to return to his room when it heard the whistle—just as a snake charmer would control a cobra.
The snake was rewarded each time."
"With the saucer of milk?" I asked, suddenly understanding another clue.
"Precisely. Now, remember the chair in Roylott's room?
He must have stood on it to reach the ventilation window.
The clang was likely the sound of the metal window being closed after the deed had been done.
However, last night, when I frightened the snake with the lit match, it retreated back up the bell rope and through the ventilation window before Roylott expected.
Not only that, but I had made the snake quite angry with my cane.
It attacked the first person it found—its master, Dr. Roylott!"
"Holmes," I replied, "if what you are saying is true, then you are responsible for the doctor's death."
Holmes just laughed and said, "I suppose that is correct, but it is not a death that I will ever regret."
When I called on my friend Sherlock Holmes after Christmas to wish him happy holidays, he was lounging on his sofa in a purple bathrobe.
On his right were a pipe rack and a pile of crumpled morning papers, evidently just read.
On his left, hanging on a wooden chair, was a very seedy, disreputable-looking felt hat that was worn and cracked in several places.
Holmes was holding a magnifying glass and medical forceps.
He pinched the hat with the forceps and lifted it to examine it under the lens.
"You're busy," I said. "I'm interrupting you."
"Not at all," Holmes said. "I'm glad you're here.
The matter at hand is trivial but still interesting."
I sat in his armchair and warmed my hands before his crackling fire.
Frosty conditions had set in, and the windows were thick with ice crystals.
"I suppose," I said, "that as ordinary as that hat looks, there's some deadly story to it, or it's the clue to some mystery or crime."
"No, no. No crime," Holmes said.
"Only one of those whimsical little incidents that happen when you have four million human beings jostling each other within the space of a few square miles.
Here in London anything's possible.
Many problems can be peculiar, however, without being criminal, as we've seen before."
"That's true," I agreed. "Half of your last six cases involved no crime."
"Precisely," said Holmes. "And I think this small matter should fall into the same innocent category.
You know Peterson, the security guard?"
"Yes."
"This evidence belongs to him."
"It's his hat?" I said.
"No. No, he found it. Its owner is unknown.
But don't see it as a battered hat; see it as an intellectual problem.
First how did it get here? It arrived on Christmas morning, along with a fat goose, which is probably roasting in Peterson's oven right now.
Peterson, who we know is a very honest fellow, shared what he knows about the situation with me."
I nodded.
"At about four o'clock in the morning, Peterson was walking home from work, still in his uniform, down Tottenham Court Road.
By the light of a street lamp, he saw a tall man ahead, walking with a slight stagger and carrying a white goose slung over his shoulder.
As Peterson watched, a gang of young men stopped this stranger and an argument broke out.
One of them knocked the man's hat off."
"Anyone hurt?" I asked.
Holmes shook his head. "The man raised his walking stick to defend himself.
However, he accidentally smashed the shop window behind him as he swung the stick.
Peterson rushed to help, but the man, shocked at having broken the window and seeing someone in uniform running toward him, dropped his goose.
He ran off and vanished in the maze of small streets.
The gang also fled when they saw Peterson, and he was left with this battered hat and a delicious Christmas goose."
"Peterson surely returned the items," I said.
"My dear fellow, that's the problem.
'For Mrs. Henry Baker' was printed on a small card tied to the bird's left leg, and the initials 'H.B.' are visible on the lining of the hat.
But as there are hundreds of Henry Bakers in this city of ours, it's not easy to restore lost property to any of them."
"What did Peterson do?" I said.
"He brought me the hat and goose, knowing that even the smallest problems interest me.
Not long after, Peterson and I agreed that the bird might spoil and should be eaten immediately.
So he carried it off, while I kept the hat of the unknown gentleman who lost his Christmas dinner."
"How are you ever going to find out who owns the hat?" I asked.
"We have everything we need right here," Holmes said.
"From this old hat?" I said.
"Precisely."
"You're joking." I laughed.
"Here's my magnifying glass. You know my methods. What can you tell me about the man who wore this hat?"
I turned the tattered hat over gingerly.
It was an ordinary black hat of the usual round shape, hard and well worn.
The red silk lining was very discolored.
There was no brand name, but as Holmes said, the initials "H.B." were scrawled on one side.
