The outer part of the hat was cracked, exceedingly dusty, and spotted in several places, although there appeared to be some attempt to hide the discolored patches by smearing them with ink.
"I see nothing," I said, handing it back to my friend.
"On the contrary, Watson, you see everything.
You fail, however, to think logically about what you see."
"Then tell me what you infer from this hat."
He picked it up, gazed at it, and promptly became lost in thought—one of Holmes' peculiar habits.
"It could suggest more," he said finally, "but a few conclusions are certain, and a few others are at least probable.
It's obvious the man is highly intellectual and was financially well-off at least three years ago, but he has fallen upon hard times.
He probably drinks. That may account for the obvious fact that his wife no longer loves him."
"My dear Holmes!"
"He still has some self-respect though," he continued, ignoring me.
"He's middle-aged and has gray hair. Oh, his hair was cut in the last few days, and he uses hair cream. Also I doubt his house is lit by gas."
"You're certainly joking, Holmes."
"Not at all. Surely you can see how I got these results."
"No doubt I am very stupid, but I don't. Why do you think this man is intellectual?"
Holmes put the hat on. It fell down over his forehead and settled on the bridge of his nose.
"Size," he said. "A man with so large a brain must have [i@something@i] in it."
"And the decline of his fortunes?"
"This style of hat, with its slightly curled-up brim, first appeared in shops three years ago.
This hat is of the very best quality. See the band of ribbed silk and the excellent lining?
This man bought this expensive hat three years ago but no hat since. He's gone down in the world."
"Well, that's clear enough," I said. "What about his self-respect?"
Sherlock Holmes laughed. "He tried to conceal some of the stains on the felt with ink.
That's a sign he hasn't entirely lost his sense of pride."
"That's plausible, I suppose."
"His age and hair cream can be determined by close examination of the lower lining.
The magnifying glass shows a large number of gray hair ends, clean cut by a barber's scissors. They appear sticky. Now sniff."
I bent over the hat and inhaled. "Lime."
"A popular ingredient in hair cream," said Holmes, nodding.
"Now inspect the dust. It's not a grainy, gray street dust.
It's fluffy brown: house dust. The hat is hung indoors most of the time."
"But his wife—you said she's stopped loving him."
"This hat hasn't been brushed clean for weeks. When I see you with a week's worth of dust on your hat, my dear Watson, I shall fear you've lost your wife's affection.
No wife would allow her husband to go out like that."
"He might be a bachelor," I said.
"No, the goose was for his wife. Remember the card on the bird's leg?"
"You have an answer for everything. How do you know his house is not lit by gas?"
"One candle-grease stain, or even two, might be accidental.
I see more than five.
He comes in frequent contact with burning candles—walks upstairs at night probably, his hat in one hand, a dripping candle in the other.
Anyway, he never got these stains from a gas jet. Satisfied?"
"Very clever," I said, laughing.
"But since no crime was committed and no harm done except for the loss of a goose, all this seems to be a waste of energy."
As Sherlock Holmes opened his mouth to reply, his door flew open.
Peterson rushed in, his cheeks bright red.
"The goose, Mr. Holmes!"
"The goose, sir!" Peterson had the face of a man dazed with astonishment.
"What of it? Did the bird return to life and flap through the kitchen window?"
Holmes leaned over the back of the sofa to get a better view of the man's excited face.
"See here, sir! Look what my wife found in the bird's gullet!" He held out his hand, opening it to reveal a brilliant blue stone.
Slightly smaller than a bean, it was so pure and radiant that it twinkled like a star in the center of his palm.
Sherlock Holmes got up and whistled.
"Peterson!" he said. "That's buried treasure indeed. Do you know what you've got?"
"A diamond, sir? Some kind of precious stone?"
"It's more than a precious stone. It is [i@the@i] precious stone."
"Not the Countess of Morcar's Blue Carbuncle!" I exclaimed.
"Precisely," said Holmes. "I ought to know its size and shape by now.
I've been reading about the theft of the stone in the newspaper every day.
It's absolutely unique, and its value can only be guessed.
The reward is a thousand pounds, but the market price must be more than twenty times that much."
"A thousand pounds! Good Lord!" Peterson plopped down in a chair and stared at the two of us.
"That's just the reward," Holmes said, "but I happen to know that the stone's sentimental value would make the countess part with half her fortune to get it back."
"It was lost, if I remember correctly, at the Hotel Cosmopolitan," I said.
"Precisely━on December 22, just five days ago.
A plumber was charged with taking the Blue Carbuncle from the lady's jewel case, which was in her dressing room.
The evidence against him seems to be strong. There's an article about it here, I believe."
Holmes rummaged through his newspapers, glancing over the dates, until at last he smoothed one page out, doubled it over, and read the following paragraph:
"‘Hotel Cosmopolitan Jewel Robbery.
John Horner, 26, plumber, was charged with removing the valuable gem known as the Blue Carbuncle from the jewel case of the Countess of Morcar.
James Ryder, the hotel manager, stated he had shown Horner to the dressing room on the day of the robbery in order that he might repair a heating grate.
He remained with Horner a little while but was soon called away.
On returning, Ryder found that the plumber had disappeared.
The bureau had been forced open and the small leather box where the countess had kept her jewel was lying empty on the dressing table.
Ryder called the police and Horner was arrested the same evening, but the stone could not be found either on his person or in his rooms.
Catherine Cusack, the maid, said she heard Ryder's cry when he discovered the theft, and she rushed into the room.
There she found everything to be as the hotel manager described it.
Inspector Bradstreet described Horner's arrest, saying, "He struggled frantically and protested his innocence in the strongest terms."
Because the prisoner had a previous conviction for robbery, the magistrate referred the matter to a higher court.
Horner was intensely emotional during the proceedings.
He fainted at the conclusion and was carried out of the court.'"
Holmes tossed the paper aside. "So much for the news account," he said.
"What possible sequence of events could lead from an empty jewel case to the gullet of a goose?
You see, Watson, our little deductions have suddenly become much more important.
Here is the stone; the stone came from the goose, and the goose came from Mr. Henry Baker, the gentleman with the bad hat and all the other characteristics I bored you with."
Holmes stood up and started to pace.
"We must find this gentleman and learn what part he played in this mystery.
Let's start with something simple━an advertisement in all the evening papers.
If that fails, we'll try something else."
"What will you say in the ad?" I asked.
"Give me a pencil and that slip of paper, my dear Watson," said Holmes.
Then he began to write: "A black felt hat and a goose were found on Tottenham Court Road.
Mr. Henry Baker may claim these items by applying at 6:30 this evening at 221B Baker Street."
"But will he see it?" I asked.
"He is sure to keep an eye on the papers," said Holmes.
"To a poor man, the loss was a heavy one. He was so frightened by his bad luck in breaking the window and Peterson's approach that his only thought was to run away.
But since then he must bitterly regret dropping the bird.
Using his name is a good idea because everyone he knows will call his attention to it.
Here you are, Peterson, run down and put this advertisement in the evening papers."
"Which papers, sir?"
"Oh, the [i@Globe, Star, Evening News, Standard@i] . . . all of them!"
"Very well, sir. And this stone?"
"Ah yes. I'll keep the stone," Holmes said.
"Thank you. And Peterson, buy a goose on the way back and leave it with me.
We must have one to give in place of the one your family is now devouring."
When the security guard left, Holmes lifted the stone in front of the light.
"Beautiful," he said. "See how it glints and sparkles.
Of course it's at the center of a crime. Every good stone is.
Precious gems are such a favorite temptation.
With the larger and older jewels, every facet may stand for a bloody deed."
Holmes inspected the gem under his magnifying glass.
"This stone was found on an island off the coast of southern China, and though it has all the characteristics of a garnet, it is blue instead of deep red.
Not yet twenty years old, this beautiful gem already has a sinister history.
This piece of crystallized carbon has caused two murders, a fistfight, a suicide, and several robberies.
Who'd believe such a pretty trinket could lead to prison and the hangman's noose?
I'll lock it up in my safe now and drop a line to the countess to say that we have it."
"Do you think the plumber, Horner, is innocent?" I asked.
"I can't tell."
"Could Henry Baker have anything to do with it?" I persisted.
"It's more likely, I think, that Henry Baker had no idea the bird he carried was worth more than its weight in gold.
However, I'll know for sure by a very simple test, if he answers our advertisement."
"And in the meantime?"
"I can do nothing," Holmes said.
"In that case I'll be on my way, but I'll be back tonight. I'd like to see what happens next."
"Tonight then," Holmes said.
"I dine at seven. Roasted chicken is on the menu, I believe.
Perhaps I ought to ask the cook to examine its gullet."
It was a little past six when I returned to Baker Street.
As I approached the house, I saw a tall man in a knitted cap with a coat buttoned up to his chin waiting outside in the light of the entryway.
Just as I arrived, the door opened.
"Mr. Henry Baker, I believe," Holmes said, greeting the man in a friendly manner.
"Please come in and take this chair by the fire."
As I followed the visitor into the house, Holmes said, "Ah, Watson, you've come at just the right time."
Once we were inside, Holmes turned to his new guest.
"Is this your hat, Mr. Baker?" he asked.
Mr. Baker had large, rounded shoulders, a massive head, and an intelligent face that sloped down to a pointy, grayish-brown beard.
His red nose and cheeks, plus the slight tremor of his hand, reminded me of Holmes' suspicion that the man had a drinking problem.
Baker's worn black coat was buttoned high, and his collar was turned up against the cold.
Thin wrists poked out of his coat sleeves, and there was no sign of a shirt underneath.
His appearance gave the impression of a well-educated man who had fallen on hard times.
"We've kept these things a few days," Holmes said, "and looked in the newspaper for an ad in the Lost and Found section.
Why didn't you advertise?"
Our visitor looked ashamed. "Money isn't so easy to come by these days," he said.
"I figured the thugs who attacked me also took my hat and the bird.
I didn't want to spend more money in a hopeless attempt to recover them."
"Naturally. By the way, we had to eat the bird."
"You ate it?" said our visitor, half rising from his chair.
"Yes, it would have spoiled otherwise. But we have another goose for you.
It's the same weight and perfectly fresh. Will that do?"
"Oh certainly, certainly," Mr. Baker said with a sigh of relief.
"We still have the feathers, feet, and the gullet of your original bird, if you wish━"
The man burst into a hearty laugh.
"They are no use to me except as souvenirs of my misadventure," he said.
"No, sir, but I thank you. I'll just take this new bird as a replacement."
Sherlock Holmes glanced sharply at me and gave a slight shrug.
"Here's your goose and your hat," Holmes said.
"By the way, where did you get the other bird? I like good poultry, and I haven't seen a better goose."
Baker stood and tucked his newly gained property under his arm.
"My friends and I frequent the Alpha Inn. This year Windigate, the owner, started a goose club.
We pay a little bit every week, and at Christmas we each get a bird.
I was all paid up, but you know the rest. I'm indebted to you, sir.
This knitted cap doesn't fit my age or style." He switched hats and, with comical pomposity, bowed solemnly and strode off.
"So much for Mr. Henry Baker," Holmes said after the door closed.
"It's obvious he knows nothing about the Blue Carbuncle. Are you hungry, Watson?"
"Not particularly."
"Let's skip dinner and follow this clue while it's still hot."
"By all means," I agreed.
It was bitterly cold, so we put on woolen scarves and heavy coats.
Outside, the stars shone in a cloudless sky, while the breath of the passersby blew out like gun smoke.
Our footsteps echoed crisp and loud as we swung through Wimpole Street, Harley Street, and onto Oxford Street.
Fifteen minutes later we were at the Alpha Inn, a small corner bar.
Holmes pushed open the door and ordered two beers from the ruddy-faced, aproned bartender.
"Your beer will be excellent if it's as good as your geese," Holmes said.
"My geese!" The man seemed surprised.
"Yes. I just met a member of your goose club."
"Oh, I see. But they aren't our geese," the bartender said.
"Whose are they then?"
"We buy them from a salesman in Covent Garden."
"I know some of them. Which one was it?" Holmes asked casually.
"Breckinridge is his name."
"Hmm, I don't know him," said Holmes, tipping the bartender.
"Well, here's to your good fortune, sir. Good night."
"Let's find Mr. Breckinridge," said Holmes as we left the bar and went out into the frosty air.
"Remember, Watson, there's a goose at one end of this mystery, but at the other end is a man who will spend seven years in jail unless we prove his innocence."
"We may discover he's guilty," I said.
"Yes, but we know something the police don't. It may be his only chance. Let's follow this lead to the end!"
We crossed Holborn Street and strode through a zig-zag of slums to Covent Garden Farmer's Market.
The largest stall said "Breckinridge," and inside, a man with a horselike face was helping a boy close up for the night.
"Good evening, sir. Cold, isn't it?" said Holmes.
The salesman nodded and shot a questioning glance at my companion.
"Sold out of geese, I see." Holmes pointed to the bare slabs of marble.
"There'll be more tomorrow morning," said Breckinridge.
"That's no good," Holmes said.
"Well, try the next stall." The man pointed.
"But you were highly recommended by the bartender at the Alpha Inn," Holmes said.
"Oh yes, I sent him a couple of dozen."
"Fine birds. Where did you get them?" Holmes asked.
To my surprise the question provoked a burst of anger from the salesman.
"All right, mister." He glared and folded his arms. "What do you want?"
"Simply I'd like to know who sold you the geese you gave to the Alpha."
"I won't tell you!"
"Oh well, it's not important. But why are you so angry?"
"You'd be angry too if you'd been pestered about it as much as I have.

Holmes reached into his pocket. "But I'll bet this coin."
The salesman chuckled grimly. "Bring me the books, Bill."
The boy brought over a thin notebook and a fat accounting ledger, and opened them under a hanging lamp.
"Now then, Mr. Know-it-all," the salesman said.
"See this little book? It lists my suppliers. See that third name? Read it."
"‘Mrs. Oakshott, 117 Brixton Road,'" read Holmes.
"A town address obviously. Now find the next-to-last page in that ledger."
Holmes found it.
"Now what's the last entry?"
"‘December 22, twenty-four geese purchased from Mrs. Oakshott,'" Holmes read.
"And underneath?" the salesman prompted.
"‘Sold to Mr. Windigate of the Alpha.'"
"What do you say now?" said Breckinridge.

A few yards off, he stopped and laughed silently.
"Ah, Watson, the horse-racing sheet sticking out of his pocket told me he likes to gamble.
We couldn't have paid him to tell us, but we got all our information by making a bet.
Well, Watson, the end is near. Do we see this Mrs. Oakshott tonight or tomorrow? It's clear someone else━"
He stopped talking suddenly. A loud commotion had broken out in the stall we'd just left.
We turned and saw Breckinridge shaking his fists at a little rat-faced man.
"Those blasted geese!" the salesman shouted.
"Don't bother me anymore, or I'll set my dog on you! I bought the geese from Mrs. Oakshott, not you."
"No, but one was mine all the same," the little man whined.
"Ask Mrs. Oakshott for it."
"She said you had it."
"Get out!" Breckinridge rushed toward him, but the little man ran away.
"Ha! This may save us a trip," whispered Holmes. He raced through the crowd that had gathered, overtook the little man, and touched his shoulder.
Frightened, the rat-faced man turned around. "What do you want?" he croaked.
"Excuse me," Holmes said, "but I overheard you at Breckinridge's. I can help."
"Who are you? What could you know about it?"
"My name is Sherlock Holmes. It is my business to know what other people don't know.
You're trying to trace some geese sold by Mrs. Oakshott to Breckinridge, which then went to Mr. Windigate at the Alpha.
Windigate gave one to his club member Mr. Henry Baker."
"You can help!" cried the little fellow, with quivering fingers.
Sherlock Holmes hailed a passing cab. "We'd better talk somewhere quiet," he said.
"But please, who are you?"
The man hesitated for an instant. "My name is John Robinson."
"No, your real name," Holmes said sweetly. "It's awkward doing business with an alias."
The stranger's pale cheeks flushed. "Well . . . my real name is James Ryder."
"You are the hotel manager at the Cosmopolitan. Step in the cab please."
The little man looked half frightened, half hopeful━not sure if he was on the verge of a windfall or a catastrophe.
He entered the cab, and we rode in silence for thirty minutes until we were back at Baker Street and in the sitting room.
"Here we are!" Holmes said cheerily as we entered. "A nice, warm fire. You look cold, Mr. Ryder. Please take this chair.
Now then, you want to know about those geese."
"Yes, sir."
"One particular goose actually. A white one with a black bar across the tail."
Ryder quivered with emotion. "Oh," he cried, "where did it go?"
"It came here. A most remarkable bird," said Holmes.
"No wonder you're so interested. It laid an egg after it was dead━a very pretty and bright, little, blue egg."
Our visitor staggered to his feet and clutched the mantelpiece.
Holmes unlocked his safe and held up the Blue Carbuncle, shining like a star with a cold, brilliant, and many-pointed radiance.
Ryder glared with a tense face, uncertain whether to claim or disown it.
"The game is up, Ryder," Holmes said quietly.
Ryder gasped and staggered like a zombie toward the stone.
"Careful or you'll fall into the fire! Help him back to his chair, Watson.
He doesn't have the nerve to be a thief. Give him a sip of brandy."
Ryder sat back down with his brandy, but he stared ahead with frightened eyes.
"Let's clear up some details, shall we?" Holmes said.
"Mr. Ryder, how did you learn of the Countess of Morcar's blue stone?"
Ryder's voice cracked. "Catherine Cusack told me about it."
"I see━her ladyship's maid. You thought it would be so easy to give in to temptation and steal the gem, but you weren't very careful.
You knew the plumber, Horner, had a criminal record and that suspicion would naturally fall on him.
So you created some small job in the countess' room━you and your accomplice Cusack━and sent for Horner.
After he left, you opened the jewel case, raised the alarm, and had that unfortunate man arrested. Then you━"
Ryder threw himself down and clutched Holmes' knees. "Have mercy!" he shrieked.
"Think of my family! It'll break their hearts.
I never went wrong before! I never will again, I swear. Don't turn me in! Please, don't!"
"Get back in your chair!" Holmes said sternly.
"It's fine to beg now, but you didn't mind sending poor innocent Horner to prison."
"I'll leave the country, Mr. Holmes! The charges against him will be thrown out."
"We'll see. First how did the stone get into the goose, and how did the goose get sold? The truth is your only hope."
Ryder bit his parched lip. "I feared the police would search me and my room at the hotel, so I went to my sister's━Mrs. Oakshott of Brixton Road.
She fattens geese. She said I seemed upset. ‘Our hotel was robbed,' I told her.
Then I went into her backyard and thought about what to do."
He took a deep breath and continued.
"An ex-convict friend of mine deals in stolen goods, and he said he could sell the gem for me.
But how could I get it to him? I was worried I'd be searched and arrested with the stone in my pocket.
Geese were waddling all around my feet, and suddenly I saw how I could fool the detectives."
Ryder paused and shook his head.
"My sister promised me a goose for Christmas. I'd take it now, I thought, and hide the stone inside it.
I caught a fine, white goose with a bar on its tail, and I went behind the shed.
I pried its bill open and thrust the stone down its throat as far as my finger could reach.
The bird gulped, flapped, and struggled.
When my sister came out, the bird broke loose and fluttered off among the others.
"‘What are you doing?' she asked.
"‘Finding the fattest,' I said. ‘I'm picking out my Christmas gift.'
"‘We put your bird aside already,' she said.
"‘Thank you, Maggie,' I said, ‘but I prefer the one I just had.'
"‘Yours is heavier,' she said. ‘We fattened it just for you.'
"‘No. I want the one I just had,' I said.
"‘Fine,' she said, a little annoyed. ‘Which one?'
"‘That white one with the barred tail, right in the middle of the flock.'
"‘Kill it and take it away,' she said.
"I did and took it to my friend. We got a knife and opened the goose, but we couldn't find the stone.
My heart turned to water at my terrible mistake. I rushed back to my sister's, but all the birds were gone.
They had been taken to Breckinridge, so I asked my sister if there was another one with a bar on its tail.
"‘Yes, there were two. I could never tell them apart.'
"I pleaded with Breckinridge, but he wouldn't tell me where the geese went. My sister thinks I'm crazy.
Perhaps I am. And now I'm branded a thief without ever touching the wealth I sold my character for!"
He burst into convulsive sobbing and buried his face in his hands.
We shared a long silence, broken only by Ryder's heavy breathing and the drumming of Sherlock Holmes' finger on the table.
Then my friend rose and threw open the door.
"Get out!" he said.
"Oh! Heaven bless you!" cried Ryder.
"No more words. Get out!"
Ryder jumped up and clattered down the stairs.
Holmes reached for his pipe. "We're not policemen after all.
The countess will get her precious stone back, and Ryder won't testify, so Horner will soon go free.
Look at it this way; I may be sidestepping the judge by not reporting this, but I'm also saving a soul.
Send him to jail now, and he'll be a convict for life. Besides it's the season of forgiveness."
"That's true," I said.
"And now, my dear doctor," said Holmes,
"let us tell the cook we are ready to enjoy a tastier investigation, in which a bird is also the chief feature."
To Sherlock Holmes she is always [i@the@i] woman. I have seldom heard him mention her by any other name.
It was not that he felt any emotion like love for Irene Adler.
Love was a distraction to his cold and precise mind, something that might interfere with his work.
Yet there was only one woman who intrigued him, and that was Irene Adler.
One night as I approached our rooms on Baker Street, I looked up at the windows.
The rooms were brilliantly lit, and I saw the silhouette of the great detective against the blinds.
Holmes was pacing with his head sunk upon his chest and his hands clasped behind his back.
To me, who knew his every mood and habit, it was obvious that he was working on a case.
I went up to our rooms, and he motioned me to an armchair by the fire.
"You may be interested in this," he said, tossing me a sheet of thick, pink-tinted notepaper.
"It came in the last mail delivery. Read it aloud."
The note was undated and without either the writer's signature or address. I began to read:
"There will call upon you tonight at quarter to eight o'clock a gentleman who desires to consult you upon a matter of the greatest importance.
Your recent services to a royal house of Europe have shown that you may be safely trusted.
This account of you we have from all quarters received.
Be in your chamber at that hour, and do not be offended if your visitor wears a mask."
"This is indeed a mystery," I said. "What do you think it means?"
"I have no data yet," said Holmes. "It is a mistake to theorize before one has data. But what do you make of the note itself?"
"The man who wrote it is wealthy," I remarked, trying to imitate my friend's thinking process.
"This paper is expensive and peculiarly thick and stiff."
"Peculiar—that is the very word," said Holmes. "It is not English paper.
From the watermark, I have been able to determine that the paper was made in Bohemia."
"But who wrote the letter?" I asked.
"A man whose first language is German," said Holmes. "Note this sentence: 'This account of you we have from all quarters received.'
Only a German would be so discourteous to his verbs by leaving one at the end of a sentence. And here he comes if I'm not mistaken."
As Holmes spoke, there was the sound of horses' hooves outside, followed by the ringing of our doorbell.
While our landlady answered the door, Holmes looked out the window.
"A nice little carriage and a pair of expensive horses. There's money in this case, Watson, if nothing else," he said.
We heard a slow, heavy step upon the stairs followed by a strong rap on the door.
"Come in!" said Holmes.
The man who entered was about six feet, six inches tall. His dress was so rich that it bordered on bad taste.
Heavy bands of lamb's wool decorated the sleeves and front of his double-breasted coat.
His deep blue cloak was lined with flame-colored silk and secured at the neck with an emerald brooch.
He carried a broad-brimmed hat and hid the upper part of his face with a black mask.
"Please take a seat," said Holmes. "This is my friend and colleague, Dr. Watson, who occasionally helps me with my cases.
And to whom do I have the honor of speaking?"
"You may address me as Count Von Kramm, a Bohemian nobleman," said the man with a thick German accent.
"That is not my real name; the important person who employs me wishes my identity to remain unknown to you.
This matter involves the king of Bohemia."
"As soon as you began to speak, I was aware of all that, Your Majesty," said Holmes, taking a seat.
The man sprang from his chair and tore the mask from his face. "You are right. I am the king of Bohemia!"
Holmes closed his eyes, seeming slightly impatient with the visitor. "Please state your case."
The king looked with some surprise at the lounging figure of the detective and began his story.
"About five years ago during a lengthy visit to Warsaw, I made the acquaintance of Irene Adler," said the king.
"The name is undoubtedly familiar to you as she is well known for her attempts to advance herself in society."
"Watson, please look her up in my index," murmured Holmes without opening his eyes.
For many years Holmes had adopted a system of summarizing newspaper articles about people and things.
As a result he could furnish information about almost any person or subject.
In this instance I found Irene Adler's biography sandwiched between that of a rabbi and a naval officer who had written a book about deep-sea fish.
"Let me see," said Holmes. "Born in the United States in 1858. A singer.
Contralto, Imperial Opera of Warsaw. Retired from singing and now living in London.
Hmm . . . I deduce that Your Majesty became entangled with this young woman, wrote her some romantic letters, and now wants to get those letters back."
"Exactly," said the king. "But how—"
"Was there a secret marriage?" Holmes asked abruptly.
"No."
"Any legal papers or certificates?"
"None."
"Then I fail to see what the problem is." Holmes closed his eyes again.
"If this woman were to produce her letters for blackmail or other evil purposes, how would she prove their authenticity?"
"My handwriting," said the king.
"That could have been forged," said Holmes.
"My private notepaper."
"Stolen," Holmes quickly replied.
"My photograph."
"Bought."
"We were both in the photograph," said the king.
"Oh, dear!" Holmes' eyes flew open. "This is very bad indeed! You were most indiscreet, Your Majesty."
"I was young—I am only thirty now—and I was only the crown prince then. I was madly in love."
"The photograph must be recovered," said Holmes. "Have you tried to buy it from her?"
"She will not sell at any price, so my agents have made five attempts to steal it.
Twice I hired burglars to ransack her house; one time we diverted her luggage when she traveled; twice she has been stopped and searched.
But there has been absolutely no sign of the photograph."
Holmes laughed. "It's quite a pretty little problem."
"But a very serious one to me," said the king reproachfully. "She intends to ruin me."
"But how?"
"I am about to be married to Princess Clotilde, second daughter of the king of Scandinavia. You may know of the strict principles of her family.
The princess herself is the very soul of delicacy. A shadow of a doubt about my conduct would bring our engagement to an end."
"And what does Irene Adler propose to do?"
"She threatens to send the photograph to the Scandinavian royal family, and I know she will do it because she has a heart of steel," said the king.
"She wants to make sure that I do not marry another woman—and will go to any length to stop me!"
Sherlock Holmes gave his royal client a piercing look.
"Are you [i@sure@i] that Irene Adler has not yet sent your photograph to the Scandinavian royal family?"
"I am certain about that." The king of Bohemia nodded gravely to Holmes and me.
"She said that she would send the photograph on the day the engagement was announced, and that will be next Monday."
"Oh, then we have three days," said Holmes with a yawn.
"That's fortunate because I have one or two other important cases right now. Your Majesty will, of course, remain in London?"
"Certainly. You'll find me at the Langham Hotel under the name of Count Von Kramm. Let me know as soon as you have made any progress."
The king sighed. "I would gladly surrender part of my kingdom for that photograph."
"That's very well, but what should I use for expenses?" asked Holmes.
The king laid a heavy cloth bag on the table. "Here are three-hundred pounds in gold and seven-hundred pounds in notes."
Holmes then asked for Irene Adler's address. "I trust that we'll soon have some good news for you, Your Majesty."
After the king left, Holmes said that we would discuss the case again tomorrow at three o'clock.
The next afternoon I was in our rooms at Baker Street at three o'clock, but Holmes had not yet returned.
Our landlady, Mrs. Hudson, informed me that he had left the house at eight o'clock that morning. I sat down by the fire to wait for him.
It was almost four o'clock when a disheveled stable groom with a red face and side-whiskers entered the room.
I was used to my friend's amazing powers of disguise, but I still had to look three times to be sure it was Holmes.
He vanished into his bedroom and soon returned, looking as respectable as ever in a tweed suit. Taking a seat by the fire, he dissolved into laughter.
"Well, really!" he finally said.
"What is it?" I asked.
"It's too funny. I'm sure you'll never guess how I spent my morning."
"I suppose you've been out to Miss Adler's house."
"Quite so, but what happened afterward was rather unusual."
Disguised as an unemployed stable groom, Holmes had quickly found Miss Adler's house, Briony Lodge.
Although there was a large walled garden at the back, the front of the house was close to the road.
From the street, it was easy to see into the spacious, well-furnished sitting room on the ground floor.
"I wandered down the street," said Holmes, "and found a stable in a lane that runs alongside the garden.
I lent the stablemen a hand in rubbing down their horses.
In return I received a few coins, some tobacco, and more information than I could use about Miss Adler and half a dozen other neighbors that I didn't care about."
"And what did they say about Irene Adler?" I asked.
"She is the daintiest thing under a bonnet, according to every man there," said Holmes.
"She lives quietly, sings at concerts, drives out at five every day, and returns at seven sharp for dinner.
She has only one male visitor, but sees a great deal of him.
He is Mr. Godfrey Norton, a dark and handsome lawyer, who calls once a day and sometimes twice."
After Holmes had heard everything the men had to tell, he began to walk up and down near Briony Lodge while he thought over his plan.
"I realized that this Godfrey Norton was evidently an important factor in the matter," Holmes said to me.
"The fact that he was a lawyer sounded ominous. What was his relationship with Miss Adler and what was the object of his repeated visits?
Was she his client, his friend or his mistress? If she was a client, she had probably already transferred the photograph to him for safekeeping."
While Holmes was trying to decide whether to remain at Briony Lodge or to visit the gentleman's office, a hansom cab arrived and a man sprang out.
Holmes noted that he was a dark and remarkably handsome man, and so assumed that he was Godfrey Norton.
"He appeared to be in a great hurry, shouted to the cabman to wait, and brushed past the maid who opened the door," said Holmes.
"I caught glimpses of him through the sitting-room window, pacing up and down, waving his arms, and talking excitedly. I saw nothing of Miss Adler."
Soon Norton emerged from the house, looking even more agitated than before.
As he approached the cab, he pulled a gold watch from his pocket and glanced at it.
"Drive as fast as you can to the Church of St. Monica!" he shouted to the cabdriver. "I'll give you half a pound if you do it in twenty minutes!"
Holmes was just wondering if he should follow when a carriage came up the lane.
The coachman was still struggling into his coat.
"As soon as it pulled up," said Holmes, "Irene Adler shot out the front door and into the carriage.
As it drove away, I heard her promise the coachman half a pound if he could reach St. Monica's in twenty minutes."
Holmes knew that he should go in pursuit of them, and luckily a cab came down the street.
"The driver looked twice at such a shabby fare, but I jumped in before he could object," said Holmes.
"It was twenty-five minutes before noon, and I suspected what was happening."
When Holmes reached St. Monica's, he hurried into the church.
In front of the altar stood the couple and a clergyman, who seemed to be vigorously scolding them.
Holmes slunk up the aisle like any other unemployed person who had wandered into a church.
Suddenly the three people turned around, and Godfrey Norton came running up to Holmes.
"Thank God!" he cried. "You'll do. Come! Come!"
"What do you mean?" asked Holmes.
"Come, man! We only have three minutes, or it won't be legal."
Norton dragged Holmes to the altar, where my friend found himself muttering responses that were whispered in his ear and assisting in the marriage of Irene Adler to Godfrey Norton.
"It was all finished in an instant," Holmes said to me.
"And then there was the gentleman thanking me on one side, and the lady on the other side while the clergyman beamed in front of us.
It was the most preposterous situation I've ever been in, and that's why I was laughing just now."
Apparently the couple had needed to marry by noon or their marriage license would not be valid.
But the clergyman had refused to marry them without a witness, so they called on Holmes for help.
After the ceremony, Holmes was surprised to see them go their separate ways, the lawyer to his office and the lady to her house.
"What's next?" I asked.
"You don't mind breaking the law?" Holmes asked.
"Not in the least," I replied.
"Nor risking a chance of arrest?"
"Not for a good cause."
"Then you are the man for the job that we will undertake later tonight," said Holmes. And with that he called for supper.
"I need to discuss our plan while we eat because there is not much time," said Sherlock Holmes as Mrs. Hudson brought in our supper.
"It is nearly five o'clock now, and in two hours we must be at Briony Lodge when Irene Adler—or rather Irene Norton—returns from her drive at seven o'clock."
"And what then?" I asked.
"You must leave that to me. I have already arranged what will occur, but I insist on one thing.
You must not interfere no matter what happens. Do you understand, Watson?"
"I'm to do nothing," I said.
"That is correct. There will probably be a little disturbance. Do not join in. The disturbance will end with my being carried into the house.
Four or five minutes later someone will open the sitting-room window. You are to position yourself close to that open window."
"All right."
"I will be visible to you, so keep your eye on me. When I raise my hand like this, you will throw something into the room and shout, 'Fire!'"
I was puzzled. "But what am I to throw?"
"This smoke bomb," said Holmes, taking a long, cigar-shaped object from his pocket.
"It's nothing very sophisticated, just a simple device that plumbers use to detect where pipes are leaking.
When you shout, 'Fire,' quite a number of people will join in.
You should then walk to the end of the street, where I will meet you in ten minutes. Have I made myself clear?"
"Quite so," I replied. "You may rely entirely on me."
"Excellent! And now it is soon time for me to prepare for the new role I have to play."
After finishing his supper, Holmes disappeared into his bedroom. When he emerged, he was disguised as an amiable clergyman.
His broad black hat and baggy trousers, his sympathetic smile and general look of benevolent curiosity all contributed to his new character.
It was not merely that Holmes had changed his clothes.
His expression, his manner, his very soul seemed to vary with every fresh part that he assumed.
The stage had lost a fine actor when he became a detective.
It was quarter past six when we left Baker Street, but it was still ten minutes before seven when we arrived at our destination.
In front of Briony Lodge, the streetlamps were just being lighted.
The house looked exactly as I'd pictured it from Holmes' description, but I was surprised at how busy the street was.

There were a group of shabbily dressed men smoking and loafing at the corner, a scissors grinder working at his wheel, two soldiers flirting with a nurse, and several well-dressed young men and women walking back and forth.
"Now where are we to find this photograph?" said Holmes as we paced up and down in front of the house.
"Irene probably does not carry it with her.
She knows that the king is capable of having her stopped and searched because he has done that twice already."
"Then where is the photograph?" I asked.
"Possibly with her lawyer or banker, but I'm inclined to think not. Why should she hand it over to anyone else?
Remember that she has resolved to use it in a few days.
It must be where she can easily lay her hands on it. The photograph must be in her own house."
"But her house has been broken into twice," I protested.
"The burglars didn't know how to look for it."
"But how will you look?"
"I will not look," Holmes said mysteriously. "I will get her to show me where she has hidden it."
"Oh, she will refuse to do that," I told him.
"She will not be able to refuse. But hark! I hear the rumble of carriage wheels. Now carry out my orders exactly as I said."
As he spoke, a carriage rattled up to the door of Briony Lodge.
When it arrived, one of the shabbily dressed men at the corner dashed forward to open the door.
He obviously hoped that the lovely female passenger would reward him with a few coins.
But he was elbowed aside by another loafer, who had rushed up with the same intention.
A fierce quarrel broke out as the two soldiers sided with the first man while the scissors grinder argued on behalf of the second man.
A blow was struck.
In an instant the lady, who had stepped from her carriage, was in the center of a circle of flushed and struggling men, who struck savagely at each other with fists and sticks.
Holmes dashed into the crowd to protect the lady, but just as he reached her, he gave a cry and dropped to the ground.
Blood was running freely down his face.
As he fell, the soldiers took off in one direction and the loafers in the other.
Some of the well-dressed people, who had watched the scuffle but not joined in, crowded in to help the lady and attend to the injured clergyman.
Irene Adler, as I will continue to call her, hurried up the steps, but she paused at the door and looked back into the street.
"Is the poor clergyman badly hurt?" she asked.
"He is dead!" cried several voices.
"No, no, there's life in him!" shouted another. "But he'll be gone before you can get him to a hospital."
"He's a brave fellow," said a woman. "They would have stolen the lady's purse and watch if it hadn't been for him.
"They were a gang and a rough one too! Ah, he's breathing now."
"He can't lie in the street," said a man. "May we bring him inside, ma'am?"
"Of course," said Irene Adler. "Bring him into the sitting room where there is a comfortable sofa. Come this way, please."
Slowly and solemnly Holmes was carried into Briony Lodge.
The lamps had been lit, but the blinds had not been drawn in the sitting room, so I could see Holmes lying on the couch.
I don't know if he felt any remorse, but I felt heartily ashamed of myself when I saw that beautiful creature kindly tending to him.
And yet it would have been the worst treachery to abandon Holmes now.
I hardened my heart and took the smoke bomb from under my coat.
After all, we were not injuring her; we were keeping her from injuring another person.
Suddenly Holmes sat up and motioned like a man in need of air. A maid rushed to the window and opened it.
At the same moment he raised his hand, and I tossed my smoke bomb into the room and cried, "Fire!"
Instantly the whole crowd of spectators joined and cried, "Fire!"
Thick clouds of smoke curled through the room and out the window.
I caught a glimpse of rushing figures, and a moment later I heard Holmes reassuring everyone inside that it was a false alarm.
Slipping through the shouting crowd outside, I made my way down the street, where I was soon joined by Holmes.
"You did that very nicely, Watson," said Holmes. "Everything is all right now."
"You have the photograph?" I asked.
"No," he answered, "but I know where it is."
Sherlock Holmes and I continued walking toward our Baker Street lodgings.
"How did you discover where Irene Adler keeps the photograph?" I asked.
"She showed me just as I said she would," Holmes replied.
"I still don't understand."
"Watson, the matter was perfectly simple." The detective laughed. "You saw, of course, that everyone on the street was an accomplice of mine."
"I guessed that was the case."
"When the fight broke out, I had some wet red paint in my palm.
I rushed forward, fell down, and clapped my hand to my face, making it appear that I'd been wounded."
"I also figured that out."
"She was obliged to have me carried into her house," Holmes said.
"And I was taken into her sitting room. I knew the photograph must be either there or her bedroom."
"But what was the purpose of the smoke bomb?" I asked.
"When a woman thinks her house is on fire, her instinct is to rush to the thing that she values most," Holmes explained.
"A married woman runs for her baby; an unmarried one reaches for her jewel box."
Irene Adler rushed to the bellpull, slid back a panel in the wall, and started to remove the photograph from a secret compartment.
When Holmes announced the false alarm, she replaced the photograph and rushed out of the sitting room.
"I haven't seen her since," said Holmes. "I was thinking about removing the photograph when her coachman came into the room.
He was watching me carefully, so it seemed safer to wait."
"What happens now?" I asked.
"Tomorrow morning at eight o'clock we'll go to Briony Lodge with the king.
We will be shown into the sitting room to wait for the lady. But when she comes downstairs, she probably will not find us or the photograph."
The detective smiled slyly. "I thought His Majesty might like to recover it with his own hands. I must send a wire to the king immediately."
At this point we reached Baker Street and stopped at our door.
Holmes was searching his pockets for the key when someone said, "Good night, Mr. Holmes."
There were several people on the sidewalk, but the greeting appeared to come from a slim youth in a long overcoat, who had hurried past us.
"I've heard that voice before," said Holmes, staring down the dimly lit street. "Now I wonder who on earth that could have been."
The next morning we were having our toast and coffee when the king of Bohemia rushed into the room.
"You really have the photograph?" cried the king, grasping Holmes by both shoulders and looking eagerly into his face.
"Not yet," said the detective.
"But you have hopes of getting it?" asked the king.
"Yes, I have hopes."
"Then let's get into my carriage and be on our way," said the king.
Once we were settled in the king's carriage, Holmes told him that Irene Adler was married.
"Married! When? To whom?"
"Yesterday to an English lawyer named Norton."
"But she could not possibly love him," protested the king.
"I hope she does," replied Holmes. "If the lady loves her husband, then she doesn't love Your Majesty.
And if she doesn't love Your Majesty, then there is no reason she should interfere with your own plans to marry."
"That's true. And yet . . . well! I only wish she had been of my own class. What a queen she would have made!"
The king fell into a moody silence, which wasn't broken until we arrived at Briony Lodge.
The door of the house was open, and an elderly woman stood upon the steps.
She watched us with a sardonic eye as we alighted from the king's carriage.
"Mr. Sherlock Holmes?" she said.
"I am Mr. Holmes," replied my friend, looking rather startled.
"My mistress said you were likely to call," said the woman.
"She left this morning with her husband by the 5:15 train from Charing Cross station. They were heading somewhere in Europe, never to return."
"The photograph!" cried the king. "All is lost."
Holmes pushed past the servant, followed by the king and myself.
He rushed to the bellpull, slid back the wall panel, and, plunging in his hand, pulled out a photograph and a letter.
The photograph was of Irene Adler alone.
The letter was addressed to Sherlock Holmes.
My friend tore it open and the three of us read it together. It was dated at midnight and contained the following message:
[i@My dear Mr. Sherlock Holmes:@i]
[i@Your disguise fooled me completely. I was not suspicious until after the cry of fire.@i]
[i@But when I found I had betrayed myself, I remembered that I had been warned about you months ago.@i]
[i@I had been told that if the king employed a detective, it would certainly be you.@i]
[i@Even after I became suspicious, I found it hard to think evil of such a dear old clergyman.@i]
[i@But I have been trained as an actress myself and men's clothes are nothing new to me.@i]
[i@I sent my coachman to watch you while I ran upstairs and changed.@i]
[i@Well, I followed you to your door to be sure I really was an object of interest to the celebrated Mr. Sherlock Holmes.@i]
[i@Then I rather imprudently wished you good night and started for my husband's office.@i]
[i@We both thought the best response was to flee, especially when pursued by such a formidable detective.@i]
[i@As to the photograph, your client may rest in peace. I love, and am loved by, a better man than he.@i]
[i@The king may do what he likes without interference from the woman whom he has cruelly wronged.@i]
[i@I only keep the photograph as a safeguard against any future actions that he might take. I leave him another photograph.@i]
[i@Very truly yours,@i]
[i@Irene Adler Norton@i]
"Oh, what a woman!" cried the king. "Didn't I tell you how smart and determined she was?
Wouldn't she have made an admirable queen? It is a pity that she was not of my own class."
"From what I've seen of the lady, she seems indeed to be in a very different class from Your Majesty," Holmes said coldly.
"I'm sorry that I haven't been able to bring your case to a more successful conclusion."
"On the contrary," said the king. "I know that she will keep her word and that the photograph is as safe as if she had burned it.
Please tell me how I may reward you. This ring—" He slipped an emerald snake ring from his finger and held it out to Holmes.
"Your Majesty has something that I would value even more highly—that photograph."
"Irene's photograph?" The king stared at him in amazement. "Certainly."
"Thank you. Since there is nothing more to be done, I wish Your Majesty good morning." Holmes bowed, ignoring the hand that the king extended to him.
And that concluded the case where the best plans of the great detective were thwarted by a woman.
Holmes used to make fun of the cleverness of women, but I haven't heard him do that lately.
And when he speaks of Irene Adler, he always refers to her with honor, as [i@the@i] woman.
"From my point of view as an expert on crime," said the great detective Sherlock Holmes, "London has become a rather dull city."
He said this to me as we were finishing our breakfast one morning at Baker Street.
"I doubt you could find many citizens who would agree with you," I replied.
"I suppose you are right, Dr. Watson, and that I must not be so selfish." Holmes smiled and pushed back his chair from the table.
He was about to unfold his newspaper when we heard our doorbell ringing loudly.
This was immediately followed by a drumming sound as if a man were beating on the outer door with his fist.
"Perhaps London is about to become a little less dull for you," I remarked.
Our landlady, Mrs. Hudson, answered the door; someone ran up the stairs; and an instant later a wild-eyed, frantic young man burst into the room.
Pale and disheveled, he looked from Holmes to me, as if he were trying to determine which one of us was the great detective.
"I'm sorry, Mr. Holmes!" he cried. "You mustn't blame me for interrupting you like this; I'm nearly insane. I am the unhappy John Hector McFarlane."
He made this announcement as if his name would explain both his visit and his manner.
But I could see by Holmes' face that the name meant no more to him than to me.
"I am sure with your symptoms that my friend Dr. Watson here could prescribe you a sedative," said Holmes.
"However, I would be glad if you would compose yourself, sit down in that chair, and tell us very slowly and quietly who you are and what it is that you want.
You mentioned your name as if I should recognize it.
But I assure you that beyond the obvious facts that you are a bachelor, a lawyer, and an asthmatic, I know nothing about you."

I was familiar with Holmes' methods, so it wasn't difficult for me to follow his deductions after I observed the man's untidy attire, the sheaf of legal papers protruding from his overcoat pocket, and his labored breathing.
Our client, however, stared at Holmes in amazement.
"Yes, I am all of that, Mr. Holmes, and in addition I am the most unfortunate man in London," he said.
"For heaven's sake, don't abandon me!
If the police come to arrest me before I have finished my story, make them give me time to tell you the whole truth.
I could go to jail happy if I knew that you were working for me on the outside."
"Arrest you!" said Holmes. "This is really most gratifying. I mean, most interesting," he corrected himself.
"On what charge do you expect to be arrested?"
"Upon the charge of murdering Mr. Jonas Oldacre of Lower Norwood."
"Dear me," said Holmes. "I was only just saying to Dr. Watson that interesting criminal cases had disappeared from London."
Our visitor stretched forth a quivering hand and picked up the newspaper that still lay upon Holmes' knee.
"If you had only glanced at this morning's newspaper, sir, you would have seen why I am here," said McFarlane.
"I feel as if my name must be on everyone's lips."
He opened the newspaper and showed us the headlines: "Mysterious Affair at Lower Norwood.
Disappearance of a Well-known Builder. Suspicion of Murder and Arson. A Clue to the Criminal."
"That clue mentioned in the headline leads directly to me," said McFarlane. "I am sure the police are only waiting for the warrant to arrest me."
As he wrung his hands in agony and swayed back and forth in his chair, I looked with interest upon this young man accused of murder.
He was blond and handsome with frightened blue eyes. He seemed to be about 27 years old, and his dress and bearing were those of a gentleman.
"We must use the time we have," said Holmes. "Watson, please read this article aloud."
I picked up the newspaper and read the following:
Late last night an incident occurred in Norwood that seems to point to a serious crime.
Mr. Jonas Oldacre, age 52, is a well-known builder who resides in that suburb.
A bachelor, he has the reputation for being eccentric and secretive.
For some years he has practically withdrawn from his business, in which he is said to have made a considerable fortune.
A small lumberyard still exists behind his house, and around midnight a fire was reported there.
It was a serious fire, consuming one of the stacks of lumber, so the firemen were surprised that Mr. Oldacre did not emerge from the house.
An investigation later showed that he had disappeared from the house and his bed had not been slept in.
The safe in his bedroom was open, and a number of important papers were scattered about the room.
There were also signs of a murderous struggle. Blood was found in the bedroom and also upon the handle of an oak walking stick.
Mr. Oldacre had received a visitor late last night, and the walking stick has been identified as belonging to his visitor, a London lawyer named John Henry McFarlane.
The story continued with an update:
It is now reported that the French windows of Mr. Oldacre's bedroom, which is on the ground floor, were open.
It appeared that a bulky object had been dragged out to the lumberyard, and charred remains were found among the ashes of the fire.
The police theory is that the victim was clubbed to death in his bedroom, his papers rifled, and his body dragged out to the lumberyard, where a fire was ignited to hide the crime.
Inspector Lestrade of Scotland Yard is leading the investigation.
Sherlock Holmes listened to this remarkable story with his eyes closed and his fingertips pressed together.
"The case certainly has some points of interest," he remarked.
"May I ask, Mr. McFarlane, why you are still free since there seems to be enough evidence to justify your arrest?"
"I live at Torrington Lodge, Blackheath, with my parents," replied the young man.
"Last night by the time I finished my business with Mr. Oldacre, it was too late to go home, so I stayed at a hotel in Norwood.
I knew nothing of this affair until I was on the train and read the story in the newspaper."
He explained that he had immediately realized the danger he was in and had hurried to put his case in the hands of Sherlock Holmes.
"I have no doubt that I would have been arrested at my office or my home," he said.
"A man followed me from London Bridge Station, and—good heavens! What's that?"
It was the ringing of our doorbell that had startled our visitor, followed instantly by the sound of heavy steps upon the stairs.
A moment later our old friend Inspector Lestrade appeared in the doorway.
Over his shoulder I caught a glimpse of two uniformed policemen in the hallway.
"Mr. John Hector McFarlane?" said Lestrade.
Our client stood up with a desperate expression on his face.
"You are under arrest," said Lestrade, "for the willful murder of Mr. Jonas Oldacre of Lower Norwood."
John Hector McFarlane turned to us with a gesture of despair and sank into his chair like a man who is crushed.
"One moment, Lestrade," said Sherlock Holmes. "Don't take him away just yet.
This gentleman was about to give us his account of this very interesting affair. His story might aid us in clearing up the mystery."
"I think there will be no difficulty in clearing it up," Inspector Lestrade said grimly.
"Nevertheless, with your permission, Dr. Watson and I would be very interested in hearing his account," said Holmes.
"Well, Mr. Holmes, it is difficult for me to refuse you anything because you've helped Scotland Yard in the past."
Lestrade looked at his watch and then at McFarlane. "I'll give you half an hour."
McFarlane took a deep breath and began his story. "I must first say that I knew little about Mr. Jonas Oldacre," said McFarlane.
"His name was familiar to me because my parents were acquainted with him years ago, but they drifted away from him."
McFarlane was very much surprised, therefore, when Oldacre walked into his office the previous afternoon at about three o'clock.
Oldacre was carrying several sheets of paper covered with scribbled writing.
"Here is my will," said Oldacre. "I want you, Mr. McFarlane, to get it into proper legal shape, and I will stay here while you do so."
McFarlane began to copy it and was soon astonished to realize that he was the major beneficiary of the will.
"Oldacre was a strange, ferret-like man," said McFarlane.
"And when I looked up at him, I found his keen gray eyes fixed on me with an amused expression.
I could hardly believe the terms of the will. But he explained that he was a bachelor with few living relatives.
He'd known my parents in his youth, and he'd heard that I was a very deserving young man.
I thanked him and continued with my work, which you see here."
At this point McFarlane laid the will and Oldacre's rough draft on our table. Then McFarlane continued with his story.
"Mr. Oldacre informed me that there were a number of documents—leases, deeds, mortgages—that I should examine," said McFarlane.
"He begged me to come out to his house that night, but insisted that I not mention the will to my parents until he and I had everything settled.
He said that the will would be a nice surprise for my parents."
Oldacre suggested that he and McFarlane dine together at nine o'clock as Oldacre might not be home before then.
So McFarlane sent a telegram to his parents, saying that he had important business to attend to and that he would be late returning to Blackheath.
He went out to Norwood, but had difficulty finding Oldacre's house. It was almost half past nine when he knocked on the door.
"One moment!" said Holmes. "Who opened the door?"
"A middle-aged woman," replied McFarlane. "I suppose she was Oldacre's housekeeper."
"Please continue," said Holmes.
McFarlane wiped his damp brow and then told us that the woman had taken him into a sitting room, where a frugal supper was laid out.
After supper Oldacre showed McFarlane into his bedroom, which contained a heavy safe.
"Mr. Oldacre opened the safe and took out a stack of documents," said McFarlane. "We went over these together until eleven or twelve o'clock."
When it was time to leave, McFarlane could not find his walking stick.
Oldacre told him not to worry about that because they would be seeing a great deal of each other from now on, and he could get it the next time they met.
"Mr. Oldacre said we must not disturb the housekeeper, so he showed me out through his own French window," said McFarlane.
"I left him in his bedroom with the safe open and the papers arranged in packets on the table.
It was so late that I could not get back to Blackheath.
Thus I spent the night at the local hotel and knew nothing of this horrible affair until I read about it this morning."
"Is there anything more you'd like to ask, Mr. Holmes?" said Lestrade, who had raised his eyebrows in disbelief several times during this remarkable explanation.
"Not until I have been to Blackheath," said Holmes.
"You mean to Norwood," said Lestrade.
"Oh, yes, that's what I must have meant," said Holmes with a mysterious smile.
"Now come along, Mr. McFarlane," said Lestrade. "Two of my policemen are waiting for you in the hall."
The miserable young man stood up and, with a last beseeching glance at us, walked from the room.
The policemen led him away to jail, but Lestrade remained with us.
Meanwhile Holmes had picked up the rough draft of the will and was looking at the pages with keen interest.
"There's something strange about that document, wouldn't you say so, Lestrade?"
Holmes pushed the pages across the table to the inspector.
Lestrade looked at them with a puzzled expression.
"I can read the first few lines and some in the middle and one or two at the end, but the writing in between is very bad."
"It must have been written on a train," said Holmes. "In fact, an express train, making only one stop between Norwood and London Bridge Station.
The places where you can read the writing represent Norwood, London Bridge, and the stop in between."
Lestrade began to laugh. "Very good, Mr. Holmes, but what bearing does this have on the case?"
"It's strange that a man would draw up such an important document in so haphazard a fashion—unless, of course, he never intended to use it.
This case is not clear to me yet."
"Not clear?" said Lestrade. "What could be clearer?
The young man learns he will inherit a fortune, invents a reason to see his client that night, and kills the older man."
"It strikes me as being just a trifle too obvious," replied Holmes.
"If you were this young man, would you commit your crime on the very night after the will had been made?
Would you choose a time when the housekeeper had seen you arrive?
Would you take great pains to dispose of the body but leave your own walking stick behind?"
"As for the stick, Mr. Holmes, you know as well as I do that a criminal is often flustered and does things that a calm person would not.
McFarlane was very likely afraid to return to the room." Lestrade paused. "And there is one more thing that you should note, Mr. Holmes.
As far as we know, none of the important papers were removed from the room.
The prisoner is the one man in the world who had no reason to take them because he would eventually inherit them."
Holmes seemed struck by this remark. "I don't mean to deny that some of the evidence is very strongly in your favor," said Holmes.
"I only wish to point out that there may be another theory. Good morning, Lestrade," he went on.
"I have work to do if I am going to prove this young man's innocence."
After Inspector Lestrade departed, Sherlock Holmes made his preparations for the day. He was acting like a man who had a pleasant task ahead of him.
"My first move, Watson," he said as he bustled into his coat, "must be in the direction of McFarlane's parents in Blackheath."
"Why not Norwood, the scene of the crime?" I asked.
"Because in this case we have one strange incident coming right after another strange incident," said Holmes.
"The police are concentrating on the second incident—the murder.
But it's obvious to me that the way to approach this case is to concentrate on the first incident—the unusual will, which Oldacre made so suddenly and with such an unexpected heir."
"Would you like me to come along?" I asked him.
"No." A smile flickered across his face. "If there were a chance of danger, I wouldn't dream of leaving you behind. But I don't think you can help me here.
I trust that by the time I see you this evening, I will have been able to help this unfortunate young man."
It was late when the detective returned to our lodgings.
With a glance at his tired and anxious face, I could see that his high hopes for the day had not been fulfilled.
For an hour he played his violin, trying to soothe his own ruffled spirits.
At last he flung down the instrument and plunged into a detailed account of his misadventures.
"It's all going wrong, Watson, as wrong as it can go. For once in my life, I believe Lestrade is on the right track and we are on the wrong one.
All my instincts are on one side, and all the facts are on the other."
"Did you go to Blackheath to see McFarlane's parents?" I asked.
"Yes, and I learned very quickly that the late, lamented Oldacre was quite a scoundrel," replied Holmes.
When Holmes arrived, McFarlane's father was out in search of his son. McFarlane's mother would not admit even the possibility of her son's guilt.
But she expressed no regret over Oldacre's fate.
On the contrary, she spoke of him with such bitterness that Holmes felt she could have predisposed her son to hate and kill the builder.
"I knew Oldacre when he was a young man," Mrs. McFarlane told Holmes.
"In fact, I was engaged to him when I heard a shocking story of how he had turned a cat loose in an aviary, where it could catch and kill the birds.
I was so horrified at his brutal cruelty that I would have nothing more to do with him.
Thank heaven, I had the sense to marry a better, if poorer, man."
She rummaged in a bureau and soon produced a woman's photograph, horribly defaced and mutilated with a knife.
"This is my own photograph," she said to Holmes. "On my wedding day Oldacre sent it to me like this with his curse."
"Well, at least he has forgiven you now," said Holmes, "since he has left all his property to your son."
"Neither my son nor I want anything from Jonas Oldacre, dead or alive!" she cried.
Holmes could get nothing from Mrs. McFarlane that would help her son's case, so he moved on to Oldacre's house in Norwood.
Lestrade had left, but several of his policemen were still there.
They had just found something of great interest while raking through the ashes of the fire.
Besides the charred remains, they had discovered several discolored metal disks.
Holmes examined them with care, and there was no doubt that they were trouser buttons.
One of them was even marked with the name of Oldacre's tailor.
"I then went over the lawn very carefully for any footprints or signs of the crime," Holmes said to me.
"But the recent drought had made the ground as hard as rock.
Nothing was to be seen except that some body or bundle had been dragged to the lumber yard."
Next Holmes went to Oldacre's bedroom, where he examined the bloodstains.
The walking stick had been removed, but our client had already admitted it was his.
Holmes could see both Oldacre's and McFarlane's footprints on the carpet.
There was no sign that anyone else had been present, which did not help McFarlane's case either.
"Couldn't you find anything to benefit our client?" I asked Holmes.
"There was only one little gleam of hope," said Holmes. "I examined the contents of the safe, which had been left on the table.
As far as I could tell, the papers were not of any great value. Some of them referred to valuable deeds, but I could not find these deeds.
That may work in McFarlane's favor because—to use Lestrade's argument—the heir wouldn't need to steal documents he was going to inherit."
Before he left, Holmes decided to try his luck with the housekeeper, Mrs. Lexington.
"She could tell us something if she wanted to," Holmes said to me. "But she refused to say anything more than necessary."
Yes, she had let McFarlane in the night before. She had gone to bed at half past ten.
Her room was at the other end of the house, so she heard nothing of what passed between the two men.
She had been awakened by the alarm of fire. Her poor, dear master had certainly been murdered.
She had seen the buttons and was sure that they belonged to the clothes that he had worn last night.
She knew nothing of the papers nor of Mr. Oldacre's private affairs.
"So, my dear Watson, there's my report of failure," Holmes said. "And yet—and yet—"
He clenched his thin hands. "I [i@know@i] something is wrong. I feel it in my bones.
There is a detail that has not come out, and that housekeeper knows it.
There was a sort of sulky defiance in her eyes, which only goes with a guilty conscience. Oh, there's no use talking about this anymore!"
"Surely you are not giving up?" I asked.
"No, but unless we can establish an alternative theory, McFarlane is lost." Holmes paused. "There was one unusual thing among those papers.
Oldacre's bankbook showed that he didn't have much money, a surprising fact given that he was supposed to be a wealthy man.
His low bank balance was principally due to large checks that were written in the last year to a Mr. Cornelius."
"I wonder who this Mr. Cornelius is," I said.
"Yes, I will have to investigate the gentleman who cashed those checks," said Holmes.
"But I still fear, Watson, that our case will end with Lestrade hanging our client."
I don't know if Holmes managed to sleep that night, but when I came down to breakfast, I found him looking pale and harassed.
The carpet around his chair was littered with the early editions of the morning papers. An open telegram lay on the table.
"What do you think of this, Watson?" He tossed the telegram over to me.
It was from Norwood and ran as follows:
[i@Important fresh evidence has been discovered. McFarlane's guilt definitely established. Advise you to abandon the case. – Lestrade @i]
"This fresh evidence sounds serious," I said after reading Inspector Lestrade's telegram.
"It's Lestrade's little boast of victory," Holmes said with a bitter smile. "Eat your breakfast, Watson, and then we'll go to Norwood.
I feel as if I shall need your company and your moral support today."
In Norwood, Lestrade met us at the door of the builder's house.
"Step this way, gentlemen. I think I can convince you once and for all that it was John McFarlane who murdered Jonas Oldacre."
He led us through the house and into a dark hall.
"This is where McFarlane must have come out to get his hat after committing the crime," said Lestrade. "Look at this."
With a dramatic flourish, he struck a match and revealed a bloodstain on the wall.
As he held the match closer to the wall, I saw that it was more than a stain. It was a clearly defined thumbprint.
"Look at that with your magnifying glass, Mr. Holmes," said Lestrade. "You're aware that no two fingerprints are alike?"
"I have heard something of that kind," said Holmes, who was a well-known expert on fingerprints.
"Well then, will you please compare that print with this wax impression of McFarlane's right thumb, taken by my orders this morning?"
As Lestrade held the wax print close to the bloodstain, it did not take a magnifying glass to see that the two were from the same thumb.
"That is the final piece of evidence," said Lestrade.
"The final piece," I involuntarily echoed.
"Final indeed," said Holmes.
Something in his tone caught my ear, and I turned to look at him.
He appeared to be making desperate efforts to restrain a burst of laughter.
"Dear me!" he said at last. "Well now, who would have thought it? How deceptive appearances may be!
McFarlane looked like such a nice young man. It's a lesson for us—we should not trust our own judgment!"
"Yes, some of us are a little too sure of ourselves," said Lestrade.
"How fortunate that this young man should press his thumb against the wall," said Holmes. "By the way, who made this remarkable discovery?"
"It was the housekeeper, Mrs. Lexington, who drew the attention of one of my policemen to it.
He was on guard in the bedroom last night to make sure that nothing was touched at the scene of the crime."
"But why didn't the police see this mark yesterday?" asked Holmes.
"We had no particular reason to make a careful examination of the hall. Besides, as you can see, it's not in a very obvious place."
"No, of course not. I suppose there is no doubt that the mark was here yesterday."
Lestrade looked at Holmes as if he were insane, and I confess that I was surprised at his rather wild observation.
"I am a practical man, Mr. Holmes," the inspector said, "and when I have my evidence, I come to my conclusions.
If you have anything more to say, you'll find me writing my report in the sitting room."
Lestrade left us and Holmes turned to me with a gleam of merriment in his eyes.
"There is one serious flaw in this evidence to which our friend Lestrade attaches so much importance."
"Indeed, Holmes! What is it?"
"I [i@know@i] that mark was not here when I examined the hall yesterday. And now, Watson, let's have a little stroll outside in the sunshine."
With a confused brain but a somewhat lighter heart, I accompanied him on a walk around the garden.
Holmes looked at each side of the house. He then led the way inside and went over the whole house from basement to attic.
Most of the rooms were unfurnished, but Holmes inspected them all carefully.
Finally he paced along the top floor, where a corridor ran outside three empty bedrooms. Again he was seized with a spasm of merriment.
"It's time to let Lestrade in on some of the unique features of this case," said Holmes.
We went downstairs and found the inspector writing his report.
"I think you may be a little premature in writing up this case," Holmes said to Lestrade.
Lestrade laid down his pen and looked curiously at him. "What do you mean?"
"There is an important witness whom you have not seen."
"Can you produce him?"
"I think I can with the aid of your policemen on duty."
Five minutes later three policemen were assembled in the sitting room.
Holmes instructed them to bring inside two bundles of straw and two buckets of water. Then he led all of us up to the top floor of the house.
"Open the window, Watson," he said, speaking in low tones, "and light the straw with one of your matches."
I did as he asked, and a coil of gray smoke swirled down the corridor while the dry straw crackled and flamed.
"Now we will produce this witness, Lestrade," Holmes said softly. "On my command, everyone shout 'Fire!' Now then: one, two, three—"
"Fire!" we all cried. "Fire!"
Suddenly a door flew open out of what appeared to be a solid wall at the end of the corridor.
An old man darted out of it like a rabbit darting from its burrow.
"Yes!" said Holmes calmly. "Watson, throw a bucket of water on the straw. Lestrade, may I present your missing witness, Mr. Jonas Oldacre."
Lestrade stared in amazement at the old man. Oldacre stood there blinking in the light.
"What is this all about?" said Lestrade.
Oldacre gave an uneasy laugh, shrinking back from the furious red face of the angry inspector. "I have done no harm."
"No harm?" said Lestrade. "You have done your best to get an innocent man hanged."
The wretched creature began to whimper. "It was only a practical joke."
"A joke?" Lestrade echoed. "Take him downstairs, men."
As the policemen led Oldacre away, Holmes showed Lestrade and me the old man's hiding spot behind the wall.
"I made up my mind that Oldacre was still in the house," Holmes said.
"When I paced one corridor and found it six feet shorter than the one below, I knew he must have built himself a hiding place.
The only other person who knew about it was his housekeeper."
Holmes explained that Oldacre was in financial trouble, so his intention was to deceive his creditors by disappearing.
He wrote checks to Mr. Cornelius because that was the name he planned to use in his new life.
As his final act of vengeance against the woman who refused to marry him, he wanted to make it appear that her son had killed him.
When McFarlane was working on the documents, he sealed one by pressing his thumb into the wax.
Oldacre was able to use this impression—and a few drops of his own blood—to make the thumbprint on the wall.
"It's likely he had his housekeeper put the thumbprint on the wall," said Holmes.
"But what about the remains in the fire?" I asked.
"Probably just some poor animal," said Holmes. "At any rate, it will be Oldacre who faces a jury now, not McFarlane."
Thanks to Holmes, our client would soon be free.
Sherlock Holmes and I were sitting near the fireplace in our Baker Street lodgings.
"Would you like a pinch of snuff, Watson?" asked Holmes.
The detective held out a gold snuffbox with a large amethyst in the center of the lid.
The ornate box was such a contrast to Holmes' simple way of life that I had to comment on it.
"Where did you get this snuffbox?" I asked.
"It's a little present from the king of Bohemia in return for my assistance with the Irene Adler case."
"And the ring?" I asked, glancing at the remarkable diamond that sparkled upon his finger.
"It was from the reigning family of Holland for helping with a matter of extreme delicacy," said Holmes.
"I can't confide the details to anyone, not even you, my dear Watson."
"Are you working on anything special right now?" I asked him.
"I have ten or twelve cases that are important," he replied. "But none of them are interesting."
Holmes rose from his chair and went over to the window. "However I may soon have an interesting one. Look down there on the sidewalk."
I went over to the window. A tall young woman stood across the street.
She was wearing a black jacket trimmed with matching beads and fringe.
Her gray, broad-brimmed straw hat was accented with a red feather, and a heavy fur boa was wrapped around her neck.
"She seems to have some money, although not the best taste in clothing," I commented.
The woman nervously peeped at our windows and played with the buttons on her gloves.
Suddenly she plunged across the street and rang our doorbell. In a few moments our landlady, Mrs. Hudson, announced our visitor: Miss Mary Sutherland.
Holmes welcomed the woman and asked her to sit down. Then he studied her for a minute.
"With your poor eyesight, do you find that it's difficult to use a typewriter for so many hours a day?" he asked.
"I did at first, but now I know where the letters are without looking," Miss Sutherland said quickly.
Then, suddenly realizing what Holmes had said, she looked at him with both fear and astonishment in her eyes.
"How did you know all that about me?" she asked.
"I have trained myself to see what others overlook," said Holmes. "There is a small dent on either side of your nose that could only be made by eyeglasses.
Your dress sleeves have purple velvet cuffs. I can see a line a little above your wrist, where a typist would press her arm against the table."
"I am impressed," I said.
"I also noticed that Miss Sutherland must have left home in a hurry this morning because she is wearing two boots that do not match," said Holmes.
"Plus, one boot is fastened only at the first and second buttons, and the other at the first, third, and fifth buttons.
But never mind all this; it's my business to notice these things. Why have you come to consult me, Miss Sutherland?"
Looking a bit dazed by Holmes' powers of observation, Miss Sutherland blurted out her reasons for appearing at our lodgings.
"A friend recommended you because you found her husband after the police had assumed he was dead," she replied.
"Oh, Mr. Holmes, I wish you could do the same for me!
I have an income of one hundred pounds per year in addition to the money I make with my typewriter.
I would give it all to know what has become of Mr. Hosmer Angel."
"Why were you in such a hurry to come here this morning?" asked Holmes.
"Mr. Windibank—that is, my father—would not go to the police, and he would not consult you," said Miss Sutherland.
"He wouldn't do anything and kept saying no harm had been done. That made me so angry that I just threw on my things and came straight here."
"You and your father have different last names," said Holmes. "Mr. Windibank must be your stepfather."
"Yes, he is my stepfather. I call him my father although that sounds strange because he is only five years older than I am."
"And your mother is alive?"
