“That’s a recent decision—made early this morning, as a matter of fact.”
Holmes gave me a bitter laugh.
“I was sitting in my study in my dressing gown, thinking over the case, when the door opened and Professor Moriarty stood before me.”
I gasped and Holmes said he’d been surprised too.
“I was familiar with the professor’s appearance, but it was startling to see him in the flesh.”
Holmes explained that Moriarty was extremely tall and thin with sunken eyes and a clean-shaven face.
He had peered at Holmes with great curiosity.
“Moriarty smiled,” Holmes went on, “but there was something in his eyes that made me wish that I had my revolver close by.”
I found the rest of Holmes’ story fascinating and frightening.
Holmes had beckoned for Moriarty to take a seat.
“If you have anything to say, Professor, I can spare you five minutes.”
As Moriarty sat down, he reached into his pocket, and Holmes feared that he was reaching for a gun.
But Moriarty pulled out a notebook in which he’d scribbled some dates.
“You crossed my path on January 4,” Moriarty read aloud.
“On January 23 you bothered me.
By the middle of February, I was seriously inconvenienced by you.
At the end of March, you ruined my plans, and now in April, I find that I am in danger of losing my liberty, thanks to you.
This situation has become impossible. You must give up.”
“After Monday,” Holmes said.
“It’s been an intellectual treat for me to see how you’ve grappled with this affair,” Moriarty said.
“A man with your brain should be able to see that there can be only one outcome.
It would distress me to have to take an extreme measure against you.”
Holmes was unbothered by the threat.
“I long ago accepted that danger is a part of my profession.”
“This is not danger!” Moriarty snapped.
“It’s inevitable destruction.
You stand in the way not merely of an individual but also of a mighty organization, the full extent of which you cannot comprehend.”
Holmes stood up. “This has been a pleasant conversation, but I’m neglecting important business elsewhere.”
Shaking his head sadly, Moriarty looked at Holmes in silence.
“Well, it’s a pity,” the professor said at last.
“I’ve done what I could to warn you.
Even if you’re clever enough to kill me, rest assured that one of my men will do the same to you.
He already has my instructions.”
Holmes still appeared quite shaken as we sat in my study.
“Professor Moriarty has such a quiet manner, no one would ever suspect he’s a villain.”
“If you haven’t contacted the police, you should,” I said.
“That would be useless.
I already have proof that my death will look like an accident.”
“What has that evil genius done to you?” I cried in dismay.
“Professor Moriarty didn’t waste any time,” Holmes said.
“Around noon today I went out to do an errand.
As I crossed Oxford Street, a two-horse van rounded the corner and headed straight for me.
I sprang for the sidewalk and saved myself by a fraction of a second.”
“Did you provide the police with a description of the driver?” I asked.
“No, the van disappeared in an instant,” Holmes said.
“I kept to the sidewalk after that, but I still wasn’t safe.
As I walked down another street, a brick fell from the roof of a house and shattered at my feet.
At that point I did call the police.”
“Did they catch anyone?”
Holmes shook his head.
“They searched the house and found piles of brick and slate on the roof, ready for a repair job.”
The police tried to persuade Holmes that the wind had toppled the brick from the roof.
Although Holmes doubted that explanation, he couldn’t prove anything.
He spent the rest of the day at the rooms of his brother, Mycroft, but that wasn’t the end of his troubles.
“On my way here, I was attacked by a guy with a club.” Holmes continued calmly telling his story.
“I knocked him down, scraping my knuckles on his front teeth.
The police arrested him, but I’m sure he’ll soon be released.”
“Surely the police know that Moriarty has a gang of thugs and that he’s behind these attacks?”
“There’s no evidence to connect my attacker with the mild-mannered professor.
At the moment only Inspector Lestrade of Scotland Yard is fully aware of Moriarty’s criminal network.
And we don’t want to do anything to alarm Moriarty before Monday.”
“You must spend the night here with me,” I insisted.
“No, my friend, I’m a dangerous guest.
I don’t want my presence to lure Moriarty’s thugs to your door.”
Holmes shook his head.
“The best thing would be for me to escape from London for a few days.
Once the police have arrested Moriarty and his gang, I’ll be able to safely return.
In the meantime it would be a great help—and pleasure—if you would accompany me.”
I was flattered that Holmes had turned to me in this crisis.
“I don’t have a lot of patients right now, and my wife is away, so I’d be glad to come along.”
“Can you leave tomorrow morning?”
“Well . . . if necessary.”
“Oh, it’s absolutely necessary.
Never forget that you are facing the cleverest rogue and the most powerful group of criminals I’ve ever encountered.”
Holmes glanced at the window. “That is why I immediately closed your shutters.
“Now listen carefully because you must do exactly what I tell you.”
After Holmes gave me his detailed instructions, I tried again to get him to stay overnight.
But he insisted on leaving immediately.
“If you’ll just show me to your back door,” he said, “I’ll climb over the rear wall of your garden and leave you out of harm’s way.”
I led Holmes outside, where he scaled the wall that led to the street behind my house.
He whistled for a cab and vanished into the night.
I went back into the house and packed my suitcase.
Then I had a trusted messenger take my luggage to Victoria Station.
After breakfast the next morning, I too left my house by cab, although I used the front door.
Following Holmes’ orders, I was careful not to take the first cab—or even the second—that responded to my whistle.
I didn’t want to jump into a cab that had been lying in wait for me.
I ordered the cab to stop at the edge of the crowded market that Holmes had specified and handed the driver the fare.
Then I ran at top speed through the market, arriving at exactly quarter past nine, as Holmes had insisted.
At the curb I found the carriage that Holmes had said would be waiting for me.
Although the driver turned his face away from me, Holmes had said he would be wearing a black cloak with a red-trimmed collar.
We immediately sped off for Victoria Station.
So far everything had gone according to plan.
My suitcase was waiting for me at the left-luggage office.
I had no trouble finding the Paris express train or the first-class compartment that Holmes had reserved for us.
My only source of anxiety was Holmes himself.
The train was due to leave in seven minutes, and there was no sign of him.
I got off the train and searched among the travelers on the platform.
As I scanned the passing faces, I felt a tug on my sleeve.
I turned to find an elderly priest looking up at me hopefully.
“Help, please?” The priest spoke with an Italian accent and gestured toward a nearby porter.
“I can’t understand what he wants,” the porter said to me.
The priest said something in Italian while pointing to his suitcase and the train.
The only word I understood was “Paris.”
“I’m not certain,” I said.
“But I think he wants to be sure that he and his luggage are on the express train to Paris.”
The priest nodded enthusiastically, and I left him to work things out with the porter.
After a quick look around the station, I reluctantly boarded the train.
I was terribly afraid that something bad had happened to Holmes overnight.
Imagine my annoyance when I found the priest in the compartment that Holmes had reserved for us.
I tried to explain that he was in the wrong place, but he couldn’t understand me.
The doors to the train were shut, and the whistle blew.
As I continued to look out the window for Holmes, the priest spoke to me in perfect English.
“My dear Watson, you haven’t even said good morning to me.”
The drooping priest straightened up, his dull eyes suddenly full of fire.
“Holmes!” I cried. “You startled me!”
“We must still be careful.”
Holmes once again shrank into the character of the old priest.
“I took the trouble of disguising myself because they’re hot on our trail.”
“What do you mean?” I asked with alarm.
Holmes peered at the platform and drew my attention to a very tall, thin man.
“Ah, there is Moriarty himself!”
Looking out the window, I saw Moriarty frantically waving for the train to stop.
It was too late, however, as we were rapidly gaining speed and soon left the station behind.
“With all our precautions, we still cut it rather close.”
Holmes laughed as he took off his disguise and packed it away in a suitcase.
“Have you read the morning paper, Watson?”
“No, I didn’t have time to read anything before I left home.”
“Then you haven’t heard about Baker Street.
One of Moriarty’s men set fire to my rooms last night!
Luckily, the fire was put out quickly before it did any damage.”
“Good heavens, Holmes! This is intolerable!”
I was quite upset, but Holmes seemed neither troubled nor surprised.
“The gang probably lost track of me after their man was arrested for attacking me with a club,” Holmes said.
“Otherwise they would have known that I didn’t go home.
But they were obviously watching you and followed you to Victoria Station.
Are you sure you didn’t slip up?”
“I followed your instructions exactly,” I said with some irritation at his accusation.
“I sent my luggage to the station last night.
I didn’t take the first cab that arrived.
I ran through the market and arrived precisely at quarter past nine.
I jumped into the carriage that was waiting for me.”
“Did you recognize your coachman?
That was my brother, Mycroft!
I used him rather than some unknown person who could be bribed to reveal our destination.”
Holmes gave me a triumphant look.
“But enough about this morning. We must plan what we’re going to do about Moriarty.”
We were on the express train that connected with a boat for France.
“Surely there’s no way for Moriarty to catch us,” I said.
“My dear Watson, you obviously didn’t take me seriously when I said this villain is as clever as I am.
What would I do in this situation?”
I thought for a moment.
“Hire a special train to follow us, of course.
But we have a good head start, and the express doesn’t stop.
No matter how fast his train goes, it won’t catch up to ours.”
“Ah, but our train does make one stop at Canterbury, and the boat never leaves on time.
Moriarty will find us at the dock.”
“We’re being chased like we’re the criminals!” I grumbled.
For a few minutes, I stared out the window at the passing scenery.
“Let’s have Moriarty arrested when he arrives.”
“Absolutely not.” Holmes shook his head at my suggestion.
“That would throw away three months of my hard work.
If Moriarty were arrested, his gang would know that something was amiss, and they would scatter to who knows where.
No, we must wait until Monday when the police will arrest Moriarty and his gang.”
“Well, then what are we supposed to do? Let him catch us?”
By this point I was completely frustrated by Moriarty, and I’d never even met the professor.
Holmes’ plan was to get off the train at Canterbury, leaving our luggage behind.
When Moriarty arrived in Paris, he would note that our suitcases had also arrived.
But he would wait in vain for us to show up.
Meanwhile we would take a train to a different port, from which we would cross the English Channel.
Then we would travel to Switzerland, purchasing new clothing and luggage along the way.
So, we left the train at Canterbury, only to discover that the next train wouldn’t arrive for an hour.
I unhappily watched our first train disappear around the bend with my suitcase onboard.
Suddenly Holmes pulled on my sleeve and pointed toward a plume of smoke on the track.
“Look! He’s coming already!” Holmes cried.
A minute later an engine pulling a single car passed us with a rattle and a roar.
We barely had time to hide behind a pile of luggage.
Holmes laughed gleefully. “There are limits to the professor’s intelligence.
He failed to figure out that I would figure out his plans!”
I stood up and brushed myself off.
“And what would he have done if he had found us?”
“He would have tried to kill me,” Holmes replied, showing no emotion.
“Shall we see if we can find some lunch?”
Once again I admired my friend’s bravery as well as his skill in outwitting such a wily enemy.
That night we traveled to Belgium to further throw Moriarty off our trail.
By Monday morning we were in a French city along the Rhine River.
From there Holmes telegraphed Inspector Lestrade at Scotland Yard.
That evening we found a reply waiting for us at our hotel.
Holmes read it and threw it into the fireplace with a groan.
“What’s wrong?” I asked.
“Moriarty has escaped!
The police captured most of his gang, but the professor and some of his most dangerous men got away.
Of course after I left the country, there was no one equal to dealing with him.
But I thought Lestrade could handle a simple arrest.”
“What happens now?” I asked.
“With most of his gang in jail, Moriarty won’t have enough people to carry out his plans,” Holmes said.
“We’ve pretty much put him out of business, and he can’t return to London because he knows the police are after him.
So he’ll devote all his efforts to finding and killing me.
I think you’d better return to London, Watson, because I’m an even more dangerous companion now.”
There was no way I could allow my friend to continue to travel without me.
He was in too much danger.
We argued about the matter throughout dinner, but later that night we resumed our travels to Switzerland together.
For a week we had a pleasant journey, wandering through Alpine villages and lonely mountain passes.
While spring was arriving in the valleys below, the mountains above were still topped with snow.
No matter where we were, Holmes never forgot the danger that hounded us.
He scrutinized every face that passed us, looking for some sign of Moriarty.
One day as we walked along the edge of a lake, a large rock fell from the ridge above and rolled into the water.
Holmes instantly shot to the top of the ridge, craning his neck in every direction.
Our guide and I followed more slowly.
“There’s nothing wrong,” the guide said, trying to reassure him.
“It’s quite common for rocks to fall at that spot in the spring.”
Holmes merely grunted in reply.
But he raised his eyebrows at me, and I knew he was remembering the falling brick that had almost hit him in London.
Despite the threat of danger from Professor Moriarty, Holmes remained cheerful as we hiked through Switzerland.
He kept repeating that if he could rid the world of Moriarty, then he would cheerfully bring his career as a detective to an end.
In one village we stayed overnight at a small hotel run by a man named Peter Steiler.
The next day we planned to hike across the hills and spend the night in another village.
Before we set out, Steiler told us to be sure to see the Reichenbach Falls.
“You’ll have to make a small detour off the hiking trail,” he said, “but the view is well worth the extra effort.”
We thanked him and went on our way.
As Steiler had promised, the scenery at the falls was spectacular.
It was also frightening.
Swollen by melting snow, a river plunged into a deep chasm lined with black rocks.
“Let’s walk along the path for a better view.”
Holmes pointed ahead of us.
“It seems to go around the falls.”
On one side a cliff towered above us, while the falls churned and boomed below us on the other side.
“Be careful, the path is very narrow,” I said.
We had stopped about halfway around the falls when Holmes spotted a boy running toward us.
“He seems in a hurry,” Holmes said, “and if I’m not mistaken, he’s carrying a message for one of us.”
The boy soon reached us.
“For Dr. Watson,” he said, holding out a sheet of paper.
I took the note, which was from Steiler and written on his hotel stationery.
“Steiler says that an Englishwoman arrived at his hotel soon after we left.
She’s very ill and bleeding heavily and—oh, dear—she has only a few hours to live.”
I looked up at Holmes with concern and then continued reading.
“I’m sure it would be a great comfort for her to see you,” Holmes said.
“You must go to her at once.”
“Yes, it’s difficult to refuse anyone dying so far from home.
But I hesitate to leave you alone in this remote spot.”
Holmes waved away my concern with his walking stick.
“Don’t worry about me. I’m sure that, for the right price, this Swiss lad will be glad to stay as my guide and companion.”
The boy nodded eagerly.
“Well, if you’re sure . . .”
I was still reluctant to leave him.
“Go! I’ll stay here at the falls for a while and then walk slowly over the hills to the next village.
You can join me there later today.”
When I finally left my dear friend, he was leaning against a large rock and staring into the falls.
Little did I know that this was the last time I would ever see Sherlock Holmes.
A few minutes later, I looked back.
I could no longer see the falls, but I could see a man hurrying toward them.
I remember wondering where the man had come from, but my thoughts quickly turned back to the ill woman waiting for me.
It took me about an hour to reach our hotel, where I found Steiler standing on the porch.
“How is she doing?” I asked him.
“Who are you talking about?” He looked puzzled.
With a trembling hand, I pulled the note from my pocket.
“Did you write this? Is there a sick Englishwoman here?”
“Certainly not!” Steiler peered at the note.
“That is our hotel stationery, but I didn’t write to you.
It must have been written by that tall Englishman who arrived after you left. He said—”
I didn’t wait to hear his explanation.
I was already running down the street, heading for the hiking trail that I had just descended.
When I finally reached the falls again, I knew my fears were justified.
Holmes’ walking stick was leaning against the rock where I’d left him.
But there was no other sign of him or the boy.
“Holmes!” I shouted in every direction.
“Holmes! Where are you?” There was no response.
My heart was pounding, but I had to get control of my emotions.
“What would Holmes do?” I asked myself and then realized that the answer was obvious.
“He’d look for clues and try to figure out what happened.”
Alas, it was only too easy to do.
Holmes and I had stopped at the large rock, halfway around the falls.
The path was soft, so it was easy for me to see many footprints.
Beyond the rock, however, there were only two sets of footprints leading away from me, and none returning.
A few yards from the end of the path, the grass and weeds along the edge had been disturbed—sure signs of a struggle.
I lay on my stomach and peered into the chasm below.
“Holmes!” I called again and again.
But I heard only the echo of my own voice.
I got up and walked back to where Holmes’ walking stick was propped against the large rock.
Looking down, I saw something white sticking out from beneath a stone.
I bent over and found a piece of paper torn from Holmes’ notebook.
[i@My dear Watson,@i]
[i@If I may make a full confession . . .@i]
[i@I was convinced that the message from the hotel was a hoax.@i]
[i@But I allowed you to leave because I thought that Professor Moriarty might appear, and indeed he has arrived.@i]
[i@He has kindly permitted me to write these lines, after which we will have a final discussion of those issues that lie between us.@i]
[i@He has already given me a description of how he avoided the police and kept himself informed of our movements.@i]
[i@It certainly confirms my high opinion of his abilities.@i]
[i@I’m happy that I will be able to free society from him, but I fear my actions will cause pain to my friends and especially to you.@i]
[i@Do not be unduly distressed, my dear fellow.@i]
[i@Tell Inspector Lestrade that the papers he needs to convict the gang are in my desk in a blue envelope marked Moriarty.@i]
[i@Before leaving England I made my will and handed it to my brother, Mycroft.@i]
[i@Please accept my best wishes and extend them to Mrs. Watson.@i]
[i@Sincerely yours,@i]
[i@Sherlock Holmes@i]
There is not much more for me to say about this tragedy.
Although the local experts could not determine exactly what had happened, there was little doubt that the two men had plunged over the falls to their deaths.
The Swiss boy was never found, but it was assumed that he had been hired by Moriarty and slipped away.
Thanks to Holmes’ evidence, most of Moriarty’s men were later convicted at trial in London.
As for me, I returned to England, greatly shaken by the death of Sherlock Holmes, the best and wisest man I ever knew.

episodes.title: A Card Player and a Bookseller

subtitle.text: In the three years since the death of Sherlock Holmes, my dear wife had also died.
Thanks to my friendship with the great detective, I continued to be interested in crime.
For my own amusement and to distract myself from my grief, I often followed interesting cases.
But of course I was never successful in solving any crimes.
I think that Inspector Lestrade of Scotland Yard also missed Holmes because he sometimes visited me to discuss his latest cases.
One spring evening our topic of conversation was Ronald Adair's murder, or as the newspapers called it, the Park Lane mystery.
Everyone in London was talking about this case, which was baffling the police.
"There's no question that Adair was murdered," Lestrade said as we sat in my study.
"But I can't figure out how it was done or who did it."
"Perhaps it would help if you went over the details of the case, starting with what you know about the victim."
I poured a cup of tea for each of us. "That's what Mr. Holmes would do."
Lestrade nodded. "Ronald Adair was a wealthy young man who spent his time with the best members of society.
One thing that makes this case so puzzling is that he didn't seem to have any enemies—male or female. Everyone liked him."
"That is unusual," I said. "Go on."
"Adair belonged to three London card clubs, where he regularly played whist."
Lestrade explained that whist is a game played with a partner.
On the night Adair died, he and his whist partner, Colonel Sebastian Moran, played against Daniel Murray and Sir John Hardy.
All three men said that Adair never lost much money at cards.
"I remember reading that in the newspaper stories about the murder," I said.
"I also read that Adair and Colonel Moran had recently won a large amount of money while playing cards.
Now tell me about Adair's death."
"After playing cards Adair returned home at around ten o'clock," Lestrade said.
"His mother and sister, with whom he lived on Park Lane, were out visiting relatives.
Anticipating his arrival, the maid had lit a fire in the fireplace in his study.
The room is on the second floor at the front of the house.
Because the fireplace smoked, she opened a window.
She heard Adair enter his study, but she didn't hear anything else until Adair's mother and sister came home around eleven-thirty."
Lestrade said that when Mrs. Adair went to say good night to her son, she found his study door locked.
She called for a servant, who forced the door open.
Adair had been shot to death, but there was no weapon in the room.
On his desk were some piles of money and a list of club members' names and some numbers.
"It sounds like Adair was trying to figure out how much money he had won and lost at cards," I said.
"But why had he locked the door from the inside?"
Lestrade shook his head. "That's one of the mysteries.
It's unclear whether Adair or the murderer locked the door.
One theory was that the murderer had climbed through the window and locked the door.
But if you examine the scene, you'll see that there was no way anyone could access the window."
"Park Lane is such a busy street," I said.
"There are pedestrians on that street even at night.
I'm surprised that no one saw the murderer or heard the shot."
"That's another part of the mystery!" Lestrade threw up his hands in exasperation.
"If only Sherlock Holmes were here, he'd figure it out."
The next evening I decided to stroll down Park Lane to examine the scene of the crime.
A few people were looking up at a window while they listened to a man talking about his own theories on the case.
"That must be the window of Adair's study," I thought.
"And Lestrade was right—it's completely inaccessible from the ground.
There's no tree or downspout that anyone could climb to reach it."
I listened to the man talking about the case but quickly decided his theories were absurd.
From his manner and his dress, I thought he might be a private detective.
Turning away, I bumped into an elderly man who was standing behind me on the sidewalk.
"Oh, excuse me!" I said, knocking some old books he was carrying to the ground.
As I bent to pick them up, I noticed that one was [i@The Origin of Tree Worship@i].
Wondering if this fellow was a collector of used books, I tried to apologize.
But the old man snarled at me and hurried away with his precious volumes.
I glanced up at Adair's window again, but feeling more puzzled than ever, I headed back home.
I hadn't been sitting in my study five minutes when my maid announced a visitor.
To my astonishment, it was the book collector carrying about a dozen volumes with one arm.
"You're surprised to see me, sir," he said in an odd, croaking voice.
His weather-beaten face peered out from a frame of white hair.
I nodded. "May I ask how you knew where I lived?"
"Well, I have a conscience, sir, and I thought I'd apologize to such a kind gentleman," he said.
"I hobbled after you and saw you enter this house.
If I was a bit gruff in my manner when we met earlier, I didn't mean any harm.
I'm much obliged to you for picking up my books."
"You're making too much of a small thing," I said.
"Your books must be very important to you."
"Yes, indeed! Books are my life."
The old man's eyes lit up, and he put down his pile of treasures.
I began to wonder how I was going to get this stranger out of my house.
"You probably don't realize it, but I'm a neighbor of yours," he said, looking around the room.
"You'll find my little bookshop at the corner of Church Street, and I'd be very happy to see you there.
Maybe you collect books yourself, sir?"
He pulled a book from his pile. "Here's [i@British Birds@i], for example, in fine condition and a bargain.
As are all my other books!
Five volumes would just fill up that empty space on the shelf over there."
I turned my head to look at the bookcase, and when I looked back, Sherlock Holmes was standing there, smiling at me.
I stared at him for a few seconds in utter amazement.
Then, for the first time in my life, I fainted.
When I regained consciousness, Sherlock Holmes was bending over me with a glass of water.
"My dear Watson, I owe you a thousand apologies," said the familiar voice.
"I had no idea you would be so shaken by my reappearance."
"Holmes, is it really you?" I gripped his lean, powerful arms and knew that this wasn't a ghost or a dream.
"How did you manage to emerge alive from the Reichenbach Falls?"
"Are you sure you're well enough to hear the story?"
Holmes peered at me with a look of concern.
"My dramatic reappearance has given you a serious shock."
"I'm all right, but I can hardly believe my eyes." I rubbed them and blinked a few times.
We sat down, and I saw that Holmes was still wearing the shabby coat of the bookseller.
The rest of that individual lay on the table in a pile of white hair and old books.
Holmes' thin face looked slightly gray, leading me to conclude that his recent life had not been a healthy one.
"I'm overjoyed that you're here!" I said.
"But how did you manage to climb out of that dreadful chasm?"
"I had no serious difficulty getting out of the falls, for the simple reason that I was never in them."
"You were never in the falls? But the note you left for me made it sound like you were going to die."
"That's true." Holmes nodded.
"As soon as I saw Moriarty's sinister figure appear on that narrow path, I genuinely thought my life was at an end.
Moriarty had a desperate look in his eyes, as if he knew his time was up and he only wanted to get his revenge on me."
The two men had exchanged a few words, and Moriarty allowed Holmes to write that final note.
After leaving it under the stone, Holmes continued to walk along the path with Moriarty at his heels.
"When I reached the end of the path, Moriarty suddenly rushed at me and threw his long arms around me," Holmes said.
"We tottered on the edge of the falls, both of us about to go into the chasm.
At the last second, I managed to slip from his grip and watched as he fell to his death in the falls."
Both of us were silent for a moment, contemplating how close Holmes had come to death.
I was amazed and grateful that Holmes had managed to defeat Moriarty, but I was still puzzled.
"How do you explain the tracks?" I asked.
"With my own eyes, I saw that two sets of footprints went to the end of the path and none returned."
"I immediately realized that it would be to my advantage if everyone thought I was dead."
Holmes reminded me that Inspector Lestrade had failed to capture the most dangerous members of Moriarty's gang.
"Moriarty's death would only increase their desire for revenge," Holmes explained.
"If they knew I was alive, one of them would certainly get me.
But if they thought I was dead, I could keep my eyes on them.
Sooner or later they would make themselves vulnerable, and I could either destroy them or have them arrested."
So, with some difficulty, Holmes began to climb the cliff above the path.
Partway up he reached a ledge, where he could lie hidden.
"I watched you and the Swiss police investigate my death in a completely inefficient manner.
When you had formed your inevitable—but wrong—conclusions, you all departed for the hotel."
I frowned at his criticism. "We did the best we could.
I was distraught at your death, and the police—"
"At any rate, I was left alone," Holmes interrupted.
"I thought I'd reached the end of my adventures for that day, but I was wrong."
Suddenly a huge rock fell from above, striking the path below and bouncing into the chasm.
At first Holmes thought it was an accident.
But looking up, he saw a man peering over the edge of the cliff.
Another rock struck within a foot of Holmes' head.
"An accomplice of Moriarty's had stood guard while the professor attacked me," Holmes said.
"He had seen everything and was now attempting to finish the job Moriarty had started."
When Holmes saw the man looking over the edge of the cliff again, he decided to scramble down to the path.
Another rock sailed past him as he hung by his hands from the edge of the ledge.
Partway down he slipped and landed bleeding on the path.
That night Holmes walked ten miles over the hills in the darkness.
A week later he was in Italy.
"But who was that man watching you?" I asked.
"All I knew at the time was that he was dangerous," Holmes said.
"I've spent the last three years traveling the world, trying simultaneously to evade and capture the last of Moriarty's men.
I had only one confidant, my brother, Mycroft, whom I needed to supply me with funds."
"You could have trusted me to keep your secret."
"I apologize, my dear Watson, but it was vital that you should think me dead.
Several times I picked up my pen to write to you.
But I never wrote for fear that you would inadvertently betray me. Besides . . ."
Holmes smiled wryly. "Could you have written such a convincing account of my death if you knew I was still alive?"
I grudgingly agreed that he was probably right.
"That's why I hurried away from you this evening," Holmes explained gently.
"I'm in the midst of a dangerous case.
I feared that any show of surprise or emotion from you would draw attention to me."
"And it's this case that has brought you back to London?" I asked.
"Yes, I also learned recently that only one of my enemies remains in London.
I decided to return when I read about the Ronald Adair murder.
Something about it reminded me of one of Moriarty's men."
So Holmes returned to his Baker Street rooms, which Mycroft had preserved for him.
"I'm sorry to say I frightened Mrs. Hudson, but I think our landlady will recover.
This afternoon I found myself in my old armchair in my old rooms." Holmes smiled at me.
"All that was missing was my friend Watson, sitting in the other chair."
I was grateful for his mention of our friendship and his sympathy for my wife's death.
"Work is the best antidote for sorrow," he said, "and I have a hard and dangerous night's work for us both."
I begged him to tell more, but he put me off, saying that we had three years of the past to discuss over supper.
Holmes smiled. "That's enough to keep us occupied until nine-thirty."
"What happens then?" I asked.
"We embark upon the remarkable adventure of the empty house!"
That night Holmes and I set out on our adventure at precisely nine-thirty.
Sitting next to him in a cab was just like old times.
"Did you remember to bring your revolver?" Holmes asked.
"Of course." I patted my pocket to reassure myself that it was there.
"Good."
We rode along in silence.
I could see that Holmes' brow was furrowed, but I knew better than to ask what he was thinking.
All would be revealed eventually.
We seemed to be headed toward our old rooms on Baker Street, so I was surprised when Holmes suddenly stopped the cab.
We got out, and he looked around to be sure we weren't being followed.
Then he led me through back alleys and stable yards that I'd never seen before.
At last we stopped at the back door of a house, where Holmes let us in with a key.
The place was pitch-dark, but I could tell that it was completely empty.
The floorboards creaked under our feet, and my outstretched hand touched strips of wallpaper peeling from a wall.
Holmes' cold, thin fingers encircled my wrist as he pulled me upstairs and into a large room at the front of the house.
The light from a streetlamp shone dimly through a dirty window.
"Do you know where we are?" Holmes said, letting go of my wrist.
I peered through the window to the street below.
"Surely this is Baker Street, but why are we here?"
"Because this house commands a perfect view of our old rooms.
Look across the street. Do you recognize that fellow sitting beside the window?"
I gave a cry of amazement as I caught sight of a man silhouetted against the drawn blind.
There was no mistaking that profile.
"It's you! But how can that be?"
Holmes was shaking with laughter.
"Evidently, over the past three years, I have not lost my ability to surprise you, my dear Watson.
It really is a remarkable likeness, isn't it?
While in France I had a wax bust made of myself, and with Mrs. Hudson's help, I put it in place this afternoon."
"Why go to all that trouble?"
"Because I wished someone to think that I was there when I was really elsewhere."
"And you thought your rooms were being watched?"
"I [i@knew@i] they were being watched."
Holmes said that, with the exception of one man, all of Professor Moriarty's men were either dead or in jail.
"Knowing that I was still alive," Holmes said, "this particular man believed that sooner or later I would return to my rooms.
And today his lookout saw me arrive."
"How do you know that?"
"Because when I glanced out my window, I recognized the lookout—a minor crook," Holmes said.
"But I'm not worried about him.
My main concern is the man who hired him, a very dangerous and cunning criminal, and also Moriarty's best friend and chief of staff.
He's the one who witnessed my escape from the Reichenbach Falls and tried to kill me by dropping rocks over the cliff."
I gasped. "And he's right here in London?"
Holmes nodded. "That's the man who is after me tonight, Watson, and that's the man who is quite unaware that we are after [i@him@i]."
We stood together in the darkness, watching the people below us.
I sensed that Holmes was keenly alert and noticed that his eyes were fixed intently on the stream of passersby.
It was a bleak night with the wind whistling down the street.
At one point I observed two men sheltering from the wind in the doorway of a nearby house.
I tried to draw Holmes' attention to them, but he let out an exasperated sigh and continued staring out the window.
More than once his fingers drummed against the wall.
It was evident that the great detective was growing uneasy and that his plans were not working out as he had hoped.
As midnight approached and the street became deserted, Holmes paced the room in agitation.
I was about to make a remark when I noticed something in the lighted window across the street.
"The silhouette on the blind has moved!" I clutched Holmes' arm and pointed.
"Look! The back is facing us now!"
"Of course it has moved," Holmes snapped.
"Do you honestly think I'd expect one of the sharpest minds in England to be fooled by an immobile wax dummy?"
Holmes' time away had obviously not improved his temper or reduced his impatience with people less intelligent than himself.
"We've been in this room for two hours," Holmes went on.
"Mrs. Hudson has made some small change to that figure eight times, or once every fifteen minutes.
She's careful to make sure that her shadow never appears on the blind."
Suddenly he pulled me into the blackest corner of the room and whispered in my ear to be quiet.
The fingers that clutched my arm were quivering with suppressed excitement.
In the next instant, I was aware of what his keener senses had already distinguished.
A small noise reached my ears, not from the direction of Baker Street, but from the back of the house.
I heard a door open and shut.
Then I heard footsteps creeping up the stairs and down the hall toward us.
The footsteps reverberated harshly throughout the empty house.
Holmes crouched against the wall, and I did the same, my hand closing on my revolver.
Peering through the gloom, I saw the vague outline of a man entering the room.
The sinister figure was within ten feet of us before I realized that he had no idea of our presence.
Stealing over to the window, he quietly raised it about half a foot.
As he knelt on the floor, the beam from the streetlamp lit his face.
He was an elderly man, wearing formal evening clothes, an overcoat, and a top hat.
Instead of resembling a killer, he looked like a gentleman who’d spent the evening at the opera.
I thought he was carrying a stick until he laid it on the floor with a metallic clang.
When he pulled something from the pocket of his coat, I realized with horror he was assembling some kind of gun.
For an instant the man was motionless.
Then he cuddled the gun into his shoulder, and his finger tightened on the trigger.
There was a strange [i@whiz!@i], which didn't sound like any gunshot I'd ever heard.
But the tinkle of broken glass confirmed that he'd hit his target—the wax dummy across the street!
Holmes sprang like a tiger onto the man's back and wrestled him to the floor.
The man jumped up and seized Holmes by the throat.
"Holmes!" I cried as I rushed to his aid.
Somehow I managed to knock the gunman to the floor again, and Holmes escaped his clutches.
The stranger squirmed mightily, but I held onto him while Holmes blew a whistle out the window.
In a moment two policemen and Inspector Lestrade burst into the house and came to our rescue.
Holmes and his old friend exchanged greetings, while the two policemen pulled their prisoner upright.
"You fiend!" he shouted at Holmes. "You clever, clever fiend!"
Holmes picked up one of the policemen's lanterns and illuminated the man's face.
"Gentlemen," Holmes said, "may I introduce Colonel Sebastian Moran, one of the best shots that our army has ever produced."
The fierce old man said nothing, but glared at Holmes with a strange mixture of hatred and amazement.
Holmes calmly looked him up and down.
"Colonel, I haven't had the pleasure of seeing you since you were paying such close attention to me at the Reichenbach Falls."
Snarling with rage, Moran sprang forward, but the policemen kept him from attacking Holmes.
"I never imagined that you'd make use of this conveniently empty house," Holmes went on.
"I thought you'd attack me from the street, where Inspector Lestrade and his men were waiting.
Aside from that, everything has gone as I expected."
Colonel Moran turned to Lestrade. "There's no reason I have to listen to this man.
If you're going to arrest me, then take me away."
"Oh, don't worry, we're going to arrest you . . ." Lestrade paused dramatically.
"For the attempted murder of Mr. Sherlock Holmes."
"No, no, that's not the right charge!" Holmes was busy examining Moran's gun.
"Lestrade, I don't think you realize who you're arresting.
This is the man the whole London police force has been searching for.
You need to charge Colonel Moran with the murder of Ronald Adair."
Lestrade drew in a sharp breath and stared at the man before us.
"Ronald Adair's killer!
But how did he manage that on a street full of people?"
Holmes explained that Moran had used an air gun to shoot Adair through the open window of his study.
"I've been aware of air guns for years, but never actually encountered one."
Holmes handed the weapon to Lestrade.
"They're tremendously powerful yet relatively quiet when compared to other guns."
"So that's how the colonel was able to fire the gun without anyone noticing," Lestrade said.
Holmes nodded. "And now, Watson, if you can endure the draft from a broken window, let's retire to my rooms to talk things over."
I was delighted to see that Holmes' rooms were just as I remembered them.
There were two occupants—Mrs. Hudson, who beamed at us both, and the wax dummy, which had played such an important role in the evening's adventure.
It stood on a small table with one of Holmes' old dressing gowns draped around it.
"Mrs. Hudson, I hope you followed my instructions," Holmes said to his landlady.
"Yes," she replied.
"I always approached the dummy on my knees, so that my shadow wouldn't appear on the blind."
"Excellent!" Holmes rubbed his hands together with satisfaction.
"Did you see where the bullet went?"
Mrs. Hudson handed him the bullet, which had passed through the dummy, bounced off a wall, and landed on the rug.
Holmes threw off his shabby coat and put on his dressing gown, which he took from the dummy.
"And now, Watson, sit in your chair, and we'll discuss this case."
Holmes beckoned to the seat where I'd spent many happy hours, and Mrs. Hudson left to make tea.
"You'll be surprised to learn that Colonel Moran had a distinguished career in the army."
Holmes had no idea what had motivated Moran's turn to crime.
But by the time he had retired from the army and arrived in London, Professor Moriarty was aware of his talents.
Eventually Moran became the criminal mastermind's chief of staff.
Professor Moriarty kept the colonel supplied with money and only used him for high-stakes jobs that an ordinary criminal couldn't handle.
When Moriarty's gang was broken up, there was no evidence to connect Moran with the professor.
"Do you remember when I visited you, and I closed the shutters for fear of an air gun?" Holmes asked.
I admitted that I thought it was rather strange at the time.
"I knew that if anyone had an air gun, it would be Colonel Moran, one of the best shots in the world.
When we were in Switzerland, he followed us with Moriarty, and he's undoubtedly the man who threw rocks at me."
As long as the colonel was free, Holmes would be in danger.
